That was so noticeable that even the Toronto ' Globe ' could not pass it by, and pointed out how our laws were inefficient both as regards immigration and alien labour, and insisted that they ought to be amended. On that occasion. the '.Globe' in its issue of the 16th of May, 1904, used these words :
The stranding of a great force of Italian labourers in Montreal shows serious defects in our immigration and alien labour laws. It is stated that 5,000 more of the same class will be brought to Canada during the present season.
Well, Mr. Chairman, would you believe it. that in the annual report of the Minister of the Interior, there is not a single Italian mentioned as having come to this country. I called attention to this in the committee and pointed out to the deputy minister how we ought to have a true record in that report of the nationalities of all our immigrants, and I think I had his promise that in future that would be done. These things ought to be on record, so that we would know from time to time from what nation-rdities we draw our immigrants. In addition I find that the Montreal ' Star ' said last spring that the poor law guardians in the old countt-v had pauper children to the number of 7,000 which they thought were good enough to pass inspection in this coun-trv and which they intended sending over. Whether they have come or not, I am not aware, but these are matters we should
seriously look into, and if possible not allow any one to enter this country who would become a charge on the public as a pauper or who would be likely to swell our criminal classes. Then we had a steamer which came from the far east on board of which a man had died on the passage out and was buried at sea, and which our quarantine officers reported as all right. But one of the passengers landed in Vancouver had smallpox and died in a few days and the people of Vancouver gathered up the remaining passengers and quarantined them in that city. It will be recollected also that a railway train carrying passengers from that steamer, was quai-antined at North Bay which caused a great deal of expense to the province of Ontario. And all this might have been avoided if the quarantine officers in charge at Vancouver had done their duty and discovered that there was a man on board suffering from small-pox.
We find that the city charities of Montreal during last year deported 113 people, some of whom were sent to the United States, some to England, and some to their homes in Canada. Then. I have a report from Mr. Macpherson. the agent of the Dominion Steamship Company at Quebec, in which he says that a large number of diseased persons have been allowed to land jj.ii this country. He says that one of the clerks in this own office, as a result of mingling with those people, took trachoma, and that in the country north of Quebec there are many people affected with the same disease. He says that on the authority of the doctor. He also says that out of 80,000 immigrants who landed at Quebec fully 10 per cent were diseased persons. I do not know whether this is true or not ; but it is reported in the Montreal ' Herald ' of December 26. 1903, and that is a paper which is favourable to the government, and which would not make such report if it were not true. Then we have a report from Mr. Macdonald, an architect in the city of Winnipeg, who states that many of the immigrants who came out on the same ship that he did, came from sections in Scotland where there was small-pox, and that when they landed at Halifax and it was reported that there was no disease on the ship, thev were allowed to go where they pleased without any examination, until they got tickets to travel by the railway to their destination in the west. He also says :
Then there are a certain class of city street loafers from Glasgow, Edinburgh, London and Liverpool, who should never be encouraged to come to Canada. They are only a detriment to this country. On the boat that I came over on there was a large number of English not fit to settle here.
I do not know whether the law is strong enough to prevent such a class of people from landing on our shores. If it is not, it certainly ought to be made so, because we

have quite enough of that class of people In our cities and towns, even in a country so good as ours. No matter how scarce 'labourers and mechanics may be in the country, those men are always too busy to want a job ; and in the winter time their families have to be cared for. and they themselves have to be fed by people who are charitably disposed. We do not want to increase that class in our country. I have a letter here which was written by Mr. Parker, who was in the employ of this government during the whole of the fiscal year of 1903, and who reported up to the end of December of that year. The report which has been brought down to this House in a return which I moved for, says that Mr. ,T. H. M. Parker brought in 413 immigrants for whom he was paid $978 in the fiscal year 1902-3, and that from the 30th of June to the 31st of December 1903 he brought in 334 persons, for whom he got $761. Mr. Parker writes to the public press-I find this in the ' Mail and Empire ' of the 30th of January-that there	is three times	as much	moneyspent	in the United	Staes	for	immigrants as there should be, and that not half as many people are brought in as ought to be brought in for one-third of the money. He goes on to say that out of 17 immigrants who are there on salary,	only five are at	work ;	the	otherssimply	get agents to work for	them and
they are paid by commission. He says there was an agent in Indianapolis for five years who sent only three men into this country. I do not know whether that is strictly true or not ; but I know that Mr. Scott, in his evidence before the committee this session, said that Mr. E. P. Holmes was appointed to Indianapolis on the 12th of January, 1900. that he was there until June. 1902, and that he did not report that he had sent any immigrants into this country from that place.
Is that Captain Holmes ?
What started them ?

We did.
Mr. WKLlSON. At any rate, 1 do not think it was my hon.- friend (Mr. Scott) who started them. Of course, if that hon. gentleman claims that the government made the good times, I can only say that I trust wre shah have no more bad ones ; for, surely the government are not so wicked as to punish all the good people iu the country merely to injure some wicked Tories. Surely w*ef

shall have good times if It is in the power of the government to make them. However. I think that hon. gentlemen have too good sense to claim that they are the authors of the good times. The good times come from the increase of population in the Northwest, resulting from the good advertising that country has had. We have plenty of good land in that country, and when a man can get 160 acres of land for nothing, in a region where the crops have been splendid for a number of years, and reports of whose fertility have been spread broadcast all over the world, is it any wonder that people are coming to a country like ours ? Is it anv wonder that people take up land when they can begin ploughing the morning after they reach it ? It is not as it was in Ontario, Quebec and the other provinces, where the forest had to be cleared before anything could be planted. That land is ready for the plough. Moreover, the opposition in this House is not decrying that country, as was the custom of hon. gentlemen-opposite when they were on this side of the House.
Now, I desire to say a word-I do not wish to detain the House long at this late day of the session-as to the treatment of immigrants by the United States. The United States has many restrictions upon .immigration. For instance, it is a i>enalty under the law for any one to land a person in the United States who is not entitled to be landed according to law. And agitation is being carried on with a view to making that law more stringent. I have before me a Bill which was introduced in the last session of Congress, under which the penalty for the offence' I have referred to is made imprisonment for not less than three months and not more than two years, with a fine of $1,000. This shows the view that the people of the United States take of immigration. I understand, of course, that they are in a better position to refuse immigration than we are, having already a_ very large population. It is true they have lots of vacant land, but their population is multiplying very rapidly. They are spending more money, I think, in keeping immigrants out of their country than we are spending in bringing them in. Of course, they get a great part of that money back from the steamship companies or the immigrants, for every one has to pay $2 a head-man, woman or child-who goes into the United States as an immigrant. They have 116 officers along our southern border to prevent the entrance into the United States of undesirable immigrants. They rejected last year about 5,000-some for diseases and some for other causes. We deported, according to a report which covered about a year and half, something over 400. What became of the rest ? Are they still in our country '! It seems to me that persons that the United States will not receive because they are diseased, or paupers, or likely to become paupers, should not be allowed to stay in our country. We may have all the feelings
of sympathy that we like, but we must remember that we have a duty to ourselves and to the world, to make our country great and strong, and to do that we must protect our citizens against the contact of this kind of population.
Now, I wish to refer for a few minutes to the reports of the farm delegates who were sent to the old country. Some of these delegates, I dare say, were good men, while some were not so well adapted-I should judge from the reports-for the work required of them. I think it unfortunate that the minister should have selected all these men from one party. I do not say he should have selected a large number from the opposition. but, for the sake of the influence they would have in the old country, he should have chosen men all of whom were fairly well adapted to the business in hand, instead of choosing men to be sent to the old country merely to give them a trip and allow them to do pretty much as they like. There were 27 of these agents, and we find that they were pretty liberal with the public money so far as tips- are concerned. They paid $450.S6 of our money as tips. They paid out over $100 for accident insurance. Now, I would like to know why we should pay the accident insurance of any gentleman in this country. I have made a few extracts from the reports of these agents. I do not wish to weary the House, so I shall not read them all. The first one is that of Mr. P. Campbell. He concludes his Report by saying :

In conclusion I would advise the government not to be in a hurry to fill up this country with foreigners

I do not know whether he means Scotchmen or not.
-but to keep the land for our own people as there are thousands of British subjects who would be only too glad to come to this country.
That is about the most intelligent^ thing he says. And for that we paid $506.95. Mr. Campbell paid in tips $18 ; advertising, $121 -he must have been pretty well advertised -besides $22 for printing ; board and lodging, $172.85, and sundries, $34.65. So for sundries and tips he paid over $50. The next, gentleman we have is Mr. A. L. Hail ; he cost us $578. He says he had a good time. His board and lodging cost us $249 I will read a paragraph of his report:
While in England I had a very pleasant although busy time. I was kept moving from one town to another and in that way saw a good deal of the country. Everywhere I went I was treated with the utmost courtesy and found people very anxious to come to Canada, a great many more would have come but did not have the means.
Now that is about as important as any part of the report. I think it should have been the duty of a gentleman representing the government to the people of England, to

make a full report of what he did. But a good many of these gentlemen did not think it their duty to do so. The next gentleman I come to is Mr. M. Watts. He cost us $319, and if you add the $150 that we paid to aH of them but one-there was one the government seemed to favour beyond all others, for they gave him $250-but to this gentleman they gave $150, making $465. Here is the way he winds up his report :
The farmers there wanted the cattle embargo lifted as they want our cattle for stockers, and they want the privilege of getting our beef cattle upon arrival to feed them for three months. This would create a better price for our beef cattle.
I imagine this gentleman forgot that he was immigration agent, he thought he was representing the Department of Agriculture, and he was trying to make a place to send our cattle too, instead of getting people to come to this country. This gentleman cost this country $467 for his trip. Then we have a report from Mr. S. L. Head. He cost us $415. He says, making several recommendations :
First, that only men who have had a practical experience should be engaged as lecturers.
I do not know whether he meant that as a reflection on his colleagues. If you are going to send men, that is not the kind you ought to send.
Second, that the work should be done during the fall and winter.
Third, that a much greater effort should be made to induce the British farmers to come to Canada, and that the chief energies of the department be expended along that line.
In this matter he differs entirely with Mr. Preston's statement of a few years ago. Mr. Preston said it would not be prudent to advise farmers who were well situated in the old country, to come to Canada, because, he says, they would be generally disappointed, they would not be able to make a success in this country. He said he did not feel like encouraging that kind of immigration. As a matter of fact, I think we in Canada look upon that class of people as being the most desirable, because they are men of means who would develop the country in the right direction. Besides that, they would make good settlers, and exert the right kind of influence in the country. Therefore, I would differ materially with Mr. Preston in that matter. Next we have Mr. Robert Forke. This gentleman, while he spent $430, seems to have been economical in a good many things. But here is what he says :
In connection with my visit to the old country under the instructions of the Department of Immigration, I have the honour to report as follows :
The meetings of which there were seven were all well attended and very successful, receiving a good notice in the local papers at the differ-Mr. WILSON.
ent places visited. There was usually a pretty steady stream of callers seeking a personal interview-, and I had the privilege of hearing many expressions of approval of the steps taken by the Dominion government to disseminate ininformation about the country.
These seven lectures seem to have cost the country a good deal, each lecture cost $61. I do not know anything about this gentleman. He may be a very eloquent man or he may not; he may be well fitted for his position, but certainly his report does not indicate it. I think the minister will agree with me that these reports ought to have pointed out more fully what these gentlemen did as servants of this country in Great Britain when they are sent over there to get immigrants. We ought to have a full detailed report of what they have done. Then we have Mr. John Kennedy. He lived pretty well while he was in that country, and seems to have spent $225 for board and lodgings. Here is what he says:
I inclose the account of my expenses of the trip to the old country, which is correct to the best of my knowledge, and I hope it will give satisfaction.	,
That certainly is a very important part of the report so far as he is concerned, and I presume his account has been settled. I will read the balance of his report:
I would say as far as I was concerned the trip was satisfactory, as I found the people eager to hear from Canada on immigration. I had eighteen meetings and stood the1 rest of the time in office at Belfast. I would have had more meetings, but I had to stay in the office on account of Mrs. Kelly going to Dublin. The time was too short, we ought to have been one month earlier.
Now that is the whole of that gentleman's report, for which we paid $456. I will refer to one more of these gentlemen, Mr. John Dougan :
As requested I forwarded a few of the impressions the trip made on me.
Advertising was not well done, owing to the friction amongst local shipping agents.
The work does not seem to have been well done because the agents in the old country were not agreed about it. I suppose the minister will dismiss those who made the trouble.
Some of the places selected for the delegates were unsuitable, two of my places were in barber shops with no accommodation for visitors. Where the speakers preceded the delegates, the delegate's quarters were crowded for several days from morning till night. On the whole I think good will come of the visit. Many people told me they would take the first opportunity to sell their belongings and sail for our country.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to call your attention to another matter here. There were two or three others, but I do not think they made any recommendations whatever. Then there was Mr. Arthur Kilburn who was allowed $250 for his fee. Would the

728S
hon. minister tell us why Mr. Kilburn is paid $100 more for his services than any of the other delegates. It seems to me that he was simply like the other delegates yet the other delegates in that class only got $150. There were just a few of these delegates who spent any money in advertising. .1. H. Medcalf spent $121.05, Rev. J. L. Brown, $6.93; .Tames Dale, $24.33; John Cowan' $4.87; D. MacVicker, $26.07, and W. H. Bryce, $37.48, making a total of $221.43. We find that these gentlemen paid out in tips $448.29, for sundries, $315.61, and for accident insurance over $100. I do not think that these people should be allowed to insure their lives at the expense of the people; neither do I think that they should be allowed to spend money freely in sundries and tips. If they want to be generous they should be generous out of their own pockets. We sent over fifty-four delegates and we spent upon them $25,000. I think the deputy minister told us in the committee that he had heard from one of these delegates that he had been instrumental in bringing ten or twelve people to this country. He did not say that he had heard from any more of them. That one delegate brought in ten or twelve people, and we have paid a little over $25,000 for them. I presume that some other hon. gentlemen will have something to say, that the hon. minister will have something to say, and I expect to have something more to say on the items as they go through.	.

Before my hon. friend (Mr. Wilson) sits down I would like him to explain whether the impression I have is correct that he has adduced as proof of the greater stringency in the regulations against immigration into the United States the fact that they charge $2 a head for admission to that country. If so I would like to ask him whether that is a novelty or not.

It is not a novelty for the last two or three years. Before that it was only $1 a head but there has been an effort to make it more than it is now even as the hon. gentleman will know if he has paid any attention to what the United States people have been doing. There is a very strong feeling in the United States, if I can judge from what I read in the newspapers and from the report of the Immigrant Department at Washington, against allowing any but the very best class of settlers into the country.
I merely beg to say that this has been in force for forty years.
What, the $2 tax 1
Yes, I paid it myself in 1867 while passing through Portland on my way to Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I ought to he indebted to my hon. friend for giving the committee so much detailed information in regard to the affairs of the Department of Immigration and with a good many of his remarks I And no fault. I was glad to hear my hon. friend say that he is not disposed to quarrel with the amount of the expenditure.
I would like to state that what I said was that we would not feel disposed to quarrel with the amount if we felt sure we were getting value for it. We have some doubt about that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my hon. friend takes that position I am prepared to take the position that we do get value for it and I think there is no great difficulty in showing that. As to a number of points which my hon. friend mentioned, being mere statements of fact as to which there is no dispute, such as questions of expenditure, salaries and that sort of thing, they require no special intention on my part because they are matters of record. But, my hon. friend referred to the question of permitting immigration of such a character as is illustrated by the employment of the Italians, who came to Montreal a few months ago. I may say that such a movement is in no sense a result of the work of the immigration department, and that in the present state of the law the immigration department has no power whatever to deal with a case of that kind. In the case of persons who come into the country as they came, not by way of steamship, although a few came by steamship, but by rail as the majority of them did come, there is no power under the law at the present time to interfere with these people or to prevent them from coming into Canada. As to the extent to which we should exercise the principle of exclusion that is a matter for serious consideration. It is not a matter which particularly belongs to the discussion of the immigration question or one which is connected with the work of the immigration branch. When the facts in regard to that particular matter were brought to my attention I asked my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock) to detail an officer of his department to make an investigation, not having an officer in my own department whom I thought particularly fitted for that kind of work. Mr. King, the Deputy Minister of Labour, was accordingly sent to make an investigation. He made a report and as a result of his report a further investigation was directed to be made.
May I call the hon. minister's attention to the fact that the other day the hon. Minister of Labour said that he did not make a report, that he simply gave him a memorandum.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The memorandum was the report. I do not know why my hon. friend desires to draw a distinction between a

memorandum and a report. I do not know the difference between a memorandum and a report. Perhaps my hon. friend will explain what he means. I w-as not here when the statement was made. However, Mr. King was sent down for the purpose of ascertaining the facts, he communicated them to the minister and as a result a further investigation was directed. While X am on that point I may say that the whole subject as to the extent to which exclusion should be practised in connection wTith that class of people, that is to say persons who are not of criminal antecedents, persons wTko are not exactly in the ordinary sense of the word paupers, persons who cannot be excluded by medical examination, but persons who by reason of the fact that they may, on account of their condition and circumstances shortly after they arrive here, become a charge upon the public, is a subject that we have under consideration at the present time, and my hon. friend the Minister of labour has a Bill upon the Order Paper- I think it has been introduced-with which it is proposed to deal with the subject.
The question of the appointment of inspectors to carry out such exclusion as may be decided upon by parliament, is one which will come rather under his supervision than under mine. I believe the system of medical inspection at the ocean ports at the present time is as strict as it is practicable to make it. Dr. Bryce, formerly of the Board of Health. Toronto, has been appointed chief medical inspector of the department and under his system the immigrants landing at ocean reports are iput through a very careful and thorough examination. Under the Department of Agriculture we have the quarantine service in charge of Dr. Moutizam-bert, and under that service persons are detained for what are called quarantinable diseases. After the ships pass quarantine as having a clean bill of health, the passengers are then permitted to land, but under certain restrictions, and each passenger is required to go into a room where he is submitted to a careful medical inspection by our medical inspectors. Each man, woman and child wt1io lands in Canada, personally passes through the hands of the doctor and must be certified to as being free of disease of such character as would warrant us returning them. If persons are afflicted with disease of a somewhat trifling character, but still of such a nature as would not justify the physicians in letting them pass, we have erected a detention hospital where they are treated at the expense of the transportation companies, who pay that expense proportionately.
What proportion of the expense is borne by the steamship companies ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
At the end of a certain period an account is made up setting forth Mr. SIFTOX.
the proportion of the expenses chargeable against each transportation company.
How is that ascertained ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: By taking the total cost of treatment of all the passengers detained. I was about to say that the general expense of supervision, the salary of the chief inspector for instance, is not charged against the transportation companies. But the expense of the treatment is charged-
Is the minister correct in saying that the expense of the detention of immigrants is paid by the transportation companies ?,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The expense of treatment is.
Mr.'IIOYD. The expense of treatment and detention ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The expense of treating a patient at the detention hospital while he is there is charged against the transportation company that brought him, and if he turns out to be incurable, the transportation company is required to take him back. My hon. friend will understand that there are defects in all human arrangements. We cannot calculate the expense of a matter of that kind to a copper, but that is the general system that is carried out as carefully as it can be. It is only within the last year it has been whipped into shape and no doubt it is still susceptible of improvement, but I doubt if it is open to very much improvement so far as the actual inspection is concerned. Whatever may have been the case in former years ; and while we had a fairly good system of inspection, since Dr. Bryce took charge and got his organization into shape, the medical examination at the ocean ports is now as complete and as satisfactory as we can make it. My hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson) referred, to some statement made by a man named Parker in a letter to a Toronto paper reflecting upon the immigration service in the United States of America. The explanation of that letter is the fact that Mr. Parker's services were found unsatisfactory and were dispensed with, and as is not uncommon under such circumstances he endeavoured to take satisfaction by rendering what he thought was an unfavourable account of the work of the department in which he was no longer an official.
How long had Parker been in the service of the department ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Two or three years :	he
was a sub-agent paid by commission.
Where was he operating ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In the neighbourhood of Duluth. My hon. friend will understand that in the case of these sub-agents who are paid on commission and who have the power of giving certificates to persons in-

tending to come to Canada, the department is in considerable danger of being defrauded. and notwithstanding the greatest possible care and closest inspection, we occasionally find we have an agent who is unsatisfactory, or who, even though we cannot prove it, we may suspect has defrauded us. We had one or two cases in which we suspected a sub-agent of giving fraudulent certificates, and while it was difficult to find absolute evidence of it, yet we did what a private individual would do if he strongly suspected that he had a dishonest employee, we got rid of him as quickly and as quietly as we could. As to the agent at Indianapolis, the particular results of the work in Indiana did not come to my special attention, with regard to this matter, but I may say that the work- in Indiana for some time was not very successful. That is one of the states in which we found it extremely hard to encourage the movement. We sent a large number of sub-agents to the different states and carried on an active propo-ganda, but I am not prepared to say that they were all equally successful. In some cases the agents were successful ; in some places they were not, and in some places after they had been working for a considerable length of time success came all at once.
Did I understand the hon. minister to say that the system of inspection is so efficient now that every immigrant landing in Canada is inspected by our officers ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When the committee rose at six o'clock, I was speaking of the medical inspection of immigrants at the different ports. I was saying that at the beginning of this season we had inaugurated a system of inspection which I have reason to believe is about as perfect as we can make it. Some difficulties have been experienced from the landing of very large numbers of immigrants on the same day. We haj thought that we had abundant accommodation. but it has proved for this reason to be somewhat insufficient at Quebec and Halifax. There have 'been one or two cases in which it has been somewhat difficult for the officials to handle the numbers arriving; but I can safely say that during the present season the inspection has been pretty thorough and careful. I would be quite pleased to receive suggestions for improvement from any members of the committee who have given the matter any attention ; but the matter has received the most careful attention from the medical inspector and the deputy of the department, and the
result of their efforts has been fairly satisfactory. We are making preparations for the purpose of securing further accommodation at Quebec, Halifax and St. John, and by next season I think we shall be amply equipped for any possible demand that may be made upon us. Some remarks were made by my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson) in regard to the immigration from the United States. My hon. friend expressed the opinion that the agents in the United States were not the cause of the very large and satisfactory movement of farmers from the western and northwestern states of Canada. I readily admit that if the country for which they had to work did not offer very great inducements, it would be quite impossible for any agents, however vigour-ous or active or faithful they might be in the discharge of their duties, to bring about such a movement of population as we have recently seen. But I do not think any person who has given close or careful attention to what has been going on during the last few years, will say that the movement would have taken place to any considerable extent if the work of acquainting the people of the western and northwestern states of the conditions in Canada had not been attended to. I need not repeat what I have said to the committee on former occasions in regard to the different methods adopted in carrying on that work. The lack of knowledge which formerly existed among tile farmers of the western and northwestern states in regard to conditions in northwestern Canada was almost incredible. The most remarkable ideas on the subject prevailed amongst those people, although they were at a comparatively short distance from the boundary line. Systematic and determined efforts had to be made and were made for the purpose of acquainting them with the actual advantages of the Northwestern Canada. The people of the western states have now become fairly well informed as to our country ; but the natural result of the work that we have been doing has followed, and the American railways which are interested in preventing the movement of people to northwestern Canada, have inaugurated a very vigorous campaign. a campaign attended with the expenditure of considerable money and a great deal of energy on the part of their agents, for the purpose of checking as far as possible the movement which our people have inaugurated. We have no doubt received considerable assistance from land and colonization companies engaged in the work of selling lands in the Northwest ; but it must be remembered that most of these companies came there only two or three years ago, purchased their lands and interested themselves, because of the movement which had been inaugurated and the | information which had been supplied in the western states. From the seed thus sown they expected to reap. ?nd T have no
72S7

72SS
doubt have reaped, a very valuable reward. But I am quite clear that if we desire to maintain the movement of population from the United States to Canada, we will have to continue our organization there and make as vigourous efforts as in the past.
I would like to know whether the immigration from the States is as large this year as last.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not quite. Up to the present the difference is about 4,000 in favour of the last calendar year.
Are any of the states or the Washington government interfering to prevent our agents doing their work there ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have no information except what I have seen in the press despatches indicating that the Washington government purpose calling the attention of the British government to the fact that we have an organization in their country for the purpose of attracting settlers to Canada. Until representations reach us, I cannot say how authentic the information is or not or what shape the representations will take. But up to the present we have received nothing but courtesy from any of the United States officials with whom we have come in contact. I took a trip to the United States a year ago last January, and found no disposition on the part of the municipal authorities or prominent people of the different localities where our agencies are stationed, to prevent the operations of our agents. In the last eight or nine months however, there have been some indications that efforts have been made to get the Washington government to take action in that direction. I am not aware of any law of the United States which would enable the Washington government to take any action at present, but the committee will understand that any representations from that government, even supposing there' was no law on the statute books, would have to receive very careful consideration from us. For myself, I think that everybody who is familiar with affairs in the Northwest will agree that the movement of population from the western states to our Northwest has been of a most valuable character. Even should it fall off materially in the near future, still an enormous amount of benefit has been done to our Northwest by the settlement in that country of those industrious and progressive farmers, and the testimony of our people is universal to the effect that the class of settlers we have Teceived from the western states is of the very highest quality. With regard to the general question. I may say that any movement of population is of more or less uncertain and varying character. We find that people in one of the states are on the move this year. Next year the people of the adtvPI Tw move disnoon-d to rno-'-e:
and we find that after we have been getting [DOT] Mr. SIFTON.
settlers from any particular locality for two or three years, the flow of settlement from that district is likely to decrease, because the supply of people who are disposed to move has been, to some extent, for the time being, exhausted. In England, for instance, last year the majority of immigrants came from the neighbourhood of iLondon, and this year the larger portion came from the north of England and Scotland. The flow of immigration varies in that way, so that we have to keep continually working to have the movement kept up to its present dimensions. Respecting the work done by our farm delegates, to which reference was made by the hon. member for Lennox, the delegates were not sent to England for the purpose of making reports to us on the conditions there. Of course they did make such reports when they came back, but that was not the purpose for which they were sent. But the idea was rather, and it was well carried out, to furnish the agents we have there with men who could go into the country and talk with intending settlers, so that intending settlers might have an actual idea of what Canadian settlers were like and ir. what sort of way they carried on their operations. It was for that purpose they were sent over, and the testimony of our agents is that their work has been most valuable and that to it is due a great deal of the increase in the movement from the British Isiles last year. Of course in work of this kind, we have to vary our operations just as in certain lines of business. What is effective one year may not be another, and different methods have to be adopted from time to time to suit changing circumstances. Up to the end of the fiscal year 1903-4, the number of immigrants from all sources exceeded the number of the previous year bv something like 2,000, but I am under the impression that at the end of this calendar year the number will be slightly less. Our agents in the United States attribute the falling off in immigration from that country this year to the unfavourable season. .The season when peonle move to a new country, the early spring, turned out to be unfavourable. The spring was late in the Northwest and the means of transportation in some places were congested, and there was difficulty in getting the transportation which intending settlers require, and the reports sent back by those resulted to a considerable extent in checking the movement in the early part of the season ; and once the movement is checked, it is very difficult to make up the falling off in the later months.
Is any record kept by the officials on this side of the immigrants rejected by the United States authorities and turned back upon this country ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) means those rejected by the United

States inspectors along our boundary ? No. We have no way of checking that.

I asked Mr. Sargent, the Commissioner General of Immigration of the United States, whom I met a few months ago, as to the undesirable class of immigrants seeking entrance to the United States and the efforts of his department to prevent their entrance. I asked him if he would send me a statement of the number of immigrants rejected by his department as coming from Canada. On the 5th instant. I received a letter from Mr. John H. Clarke acting commissioner. This letter is addressed to Mr. Sargent and is forwarded to me. *It says :
Number refused admission to the United States at various Canadian border stations from June, 1903, to 31st May, 1901 : total number rejected 2,141, causes for which such exclusions were made being as follows : likely to become public charges 961, contract labourers 305, afflicted with dangerous contageous diseases 663, temporarily detained and not appearing for re-examination 11, to prevent separation of families 61. aliens seeking admission minus certificates 112, idiots and insane S-making the total of 2,441.
In view of the minister's statement just before we rose at 6 o'clock, that every immigrant coming into this country was medically inspected as to his fitness, this letter is a very serious one.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) will permit me-I explained that I /referred to this year, and that I was not prepared to make that statement with regard to past seasons.

This statement is for the present season up to 31st May 1904. It does not include the last month or two, which ' (probably would show a larger number of immigrants. Now, one or other of two things must be deduced from the statements made in this letter. Either this inspection as not being carried out as the minister [DOT]ttinks it is, or-very much more serious- we must have in Canada a class of people who are immigrating, or we must have among our own people an enormous number afflicted with contagious and dangerous diseases who are leaving our country for the United States. I hope that the former is the case, for that is something that may be remedied with comparative case. But, if fit is the latter, and if we have among our population a sufficient percentage of people afflicted with dangerous contagious disease [DOT]to supply an emigration of 653 in ten months, that is something that will require the most serious attention of the government and a very close investigation. I am always accused of speaking from a railway point of view. So, I suppose I cannot be accused of wishing to restrict immigration [DOT]into this country. No one believes more strongly than I do the necessity of proper
immigration into Canada. But I think that no one realizes more than I do the absolute necessity that that immigration shall be of the right class. . In the United States, with one boundary on the southern ocean, they [DOT]have all varieties of climate. They have the natural conditions which will enable them to assimilate with comparative ease Italians and other people from the southern parts of Europe. We cannot do that. We cannot gain any advantage by bringing *to this country weaklings from the south of Europe. If the immigration is to be successful, we must have people from the northern countries, from the strong nations of Europe. The' government, I think, owe it to the country and to themselves to take every possible precaution that, neither through their immigration agents nor-what is more dangerous as to this class of persons-through the various steamship companies, which receive a bonus for immigrants besides their passage money, are people of this class landed in this country. iAs I have said, we are very much more bound to discriminate as to the class of immigrants than is the United States. If they reject these diseased people, we ought to reject them with tenfold stringency. But, we do not seem to be doing that. We are not taking care to keep out of Canada the people who come from the southern parts of Europe, many of them afflicted with diseases which are not only dangerous to themselves but are dangerous to the people of this country by reason of their contagious character.

Before this item passes. I would like to say a word as a medical man. I have henrd no more ridiculous criticism expressed in this House at any time than the criticism made _in regard to the health of the immigrants brought into this country. I would like to say to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. [DOT]Osier), that if he would refer to his own .distinguished brother, who is probably the greatest medical man that Canada has ever produced, he would find his opinion on this matter different from that which the hon. gentleman has just expressed. I wish to tell him that if this parliament had the courage it should have, it would at once take up certain questions of public health and deal with them. They are matters of [DOT]momentous importance to this country, whereas the matters to which he refers are mere bagatelles.	.

I have not the advantage possessed by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Kendall), of being a medical man, and of being able therefore to speak with authority as to the seriousness of the charges that have been made by my hon. friend on my right (Mr. Osier), and as to the inadvisability of allowing dis-I eased persons to become residents of this ' country after they have been pronounced

unfitted to become residents of the United States. The hon. gentleman probably knows more than the corps of expert medical men who have been appointed by the United States government to pay special attention to this very matter. I think I am justified in concluding, without meaning any disrespect to the hon. gentleman, that if the United States medical authorities entertained the same opinion that he does they would not go to the annual expense of maintaining along our border and in some of our principal cities groups of expert medical examiners to inquire into the physical condition of those who are seeking admission into the United States, and of rejecting them for reasons which, in the hon. gentleman's opinion, are a mere bagatelle. I have stated before in this House, and I repeat it, that the facts which have been disclosed show a disgraceful condition of things. I do not desire to throw the entire blame upon the Department of the Interior ; I rather commend the vigilance of the United States authorities. It is to me most regrettable that we have presented to us in the official reports of the Commissioner General of Immigration of the United States an annual statement showing the number of immigrants destined for the United States, who have been booked by our Canadian route, but who are not permitted to enter the United States because of phy-sicial disability. I do not know how many dozen officials the United States have stationed along our borders. I believe 116 is the number. In addition to these they have their officials stationed at Montreal and elsewhere in our country ; and these gentlemen have it in their power to say whether immigrants who come thus far on their way to the United States shall be permitted to continue their journey and enter the United States, or whether they shall be debarred at Montreal or some other Canadian (port, and be obliged to remain in this country. I appreciate the difficulties of the situation, and commend whatever the Minister of the Interior is doing to put a stop to this unsatisfactory condition of things. But I am afraid that the hon. gentleman was not speaking advisedly at six o'clock when he said that every immigrant landing in Canada was carefully examined by expert medical men.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I referred to people who come by seaports, we have no means of checking those who come in by rail.

I am speaking of those only who come across the ocean, the immigrant class who land at our ports. I understood the hon. gentleman at six o'clock to say that all these were carefully examined by our own medical men. Of course I am not in a position to dispute that statement. But I do make the assertion, that if the statistics which my colleague has presented Mr. CLARKE.
to the House are reliable-and they are official documents bearing the approval of the United States government officials-then I say that the examination made by This government must be lax, or else the examination made by the United States medical officers must be much more rigid than that which our officials make when immigrants land at our Canadian Atlantic ports. I do not think the fact that immigrants are poor, are destitue, as long as they are mentally, physically and morally fit. should debar them ; I do not think their poverty should prevent them from getting a chance to make a living in Canada. But I do say that people who are rejected because they are suffering from loathsome diseases-
What diseases ?

I cannot tell the hon. gentleman ; loathsome diseases, the classification is ; and are not fit to become citizens of the United States, ought certainly not be permitted to remain here and become a charge upon the people of this country. If they are permitted to land and proceed as far west as Montreal on their way to the United States, they certainly should not be permitted to remain in Canada if they are rejected by the United States authorities and not allowed to enter that country. I think that is a reasonable proposition and one that will commend itself to the Minister of the Interior. Two months ago I read a statement in the House from the last official report of the United States Commissioner General of Immigration, showing that some 4,000 immigrants were debarred from entering the United States at our various border ports. I asked the Minister of the Interior what became of these people, and he promised to make a statement, if my memory serves me, when these estimates were being considered. We have not had that statement from him to-night. I cannot understand by what machinery or method these people, whose destination is the United States, are permitted to come( thus far on their journey, are then prevented from continuing their journey, and are left upon our hands, especially if they are suffering from loathsome and dangerous diseases. This matter ought to engage the attention of the minister and he ought to endeavour, if possible, to devise some means whereby these people will not be allowed to come so far on their journey. If they are not fit because of their physical and mental disabilities to enter the United States, they certainly ought not to be permitted to land in Canada ; but if they land in Canada they certainly ought not to be permitted to remain here if their condition is such as is stated by the United States offi-I eials. Now I have a report for several | months of the present fiscal year, showing the number of immigrants debarred from i entering the United States from (Canada. The return is made by ports, and I would like to

draw the attention of the minister to these statements. If he wishes I will give them to him so that he can see for himself what is contained in them, and decide what remedy might be applied to put a stop to this state of things. In July of last year, the first month of the fiscal year 1903-1904, this report shows that there were landed at Quebec and St. John 3,241 immigrants, and of this number 77 were debarred, and of these 57 were suffering from loathsome or dangerous contagious diseases-these are the words used in the heading. I do not know what these diseases are. I do not know who the persons were ; but these are official returns from the United States immigration department. Now what I am drawing to the attention of the minister is the fact that year after year there is published a statement showing the number of these immigrants from Europe wending their way to the United States through Canada, who are prohibited from continuing their journey and who are left stranded in Canada.
What is to be done with these people ? Can there not be an improvement made ir the medical examination ? Can that medical examination not be made more rigid, so that they will not be allowed to land at Halifax, St. John or Quebec, or whatever the port is ? I will not weary the committee by reading all these returns that I have from month to month up to the 1st of May, but f want to draw the hon. minister's attention to the fact that in these monthly statements there are figures showing the number rejected at Vancouver as well as at Quebec and St. John. The figures for the other ports are not given in these tables. In some of the months the number rejected at Vancouver is considerable. In the month of July the number rejected was 6, in August the number rejected was IS, in September the number rejected was 25, and I may tell my hon. friend from Cape Breton that of the 25, 11 are classified as suffering from loathsome or dangerous contagious diseases. In October the number rejected was 18, in November 28, and so on. These tables show that in the six or eight months for which I have returns' hundreds of immigrants have been rejected, have been debarred from entering the United States because they have been physically unfit. 1 do not know whether the diseases from which they are .suffering are loathsome and contagious-I hope they are not for the sake of this country, because these people are left here-but I repeat the statement that they are debarred because of their physical condition. because they are classified as suffering from loathsome or dangerous contagious diseases, and it is not right that these unfortunate people should be maintained at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada, when they are immigrants destined for the United States, who are prevented from entering that country by the corps of United States officers who are doing duty at the 232
ports of Canada and along our border. We have brought this matter to the attention of the hon. minister again and again, and while we recognize that he has been appointing some medical gentlemen to intercept the flow of. these people, yet from the statement which my colleague has presented to the House, and from the figures contained in the statements which I have in my hand, there is certainly a great deal more to be done in this matter. I am sure the hon. minister will admit that if these figures are correct the situation is not a satisfactory one. We Should be able to exercise as rigid a supervision over the immigration coming into Canada as is exercised by the United States officials over the immigration going into that country. People who are debarred because of their physical disabilities, and who are not fitted to become citizens of the United States-who are not good enough, if I may be permitted to use that expression without intending to use it in the offensive sense, to become citizens of the United States-are certainly not good enough for Canada. It is quality that we should aim at rather than quantity, but if we are to have quantity-and we have room for a great many immigrants in this country-ws should certainly see to it that the necessary moneys are expended to enable us to make our medical examination of all immigrants as rigid as it is possible to make it. There is another phase of this matter, but probably I had better leave that until the discussion of this question is concluded. I shall be glad to place these statements in the possession of the hon. minister, and if I have misappr-hended what their purport is, I shall be glad to be corrected ; but in view of these statements, and in view of the statements which my colleague has presented, I think there is a screw loose yet, and I hope the hon. gentleman will see how urgent is the necessity that our system of inspection shall be equal to that which prevails along the border on the part of the immigration officials of the United States.

I do not wish to be misunderstood. I fully agree in all the arrangements that are made to provide necessary quarantine at the ports of debarcation, but I repeat that if the few scores or few hundreds of infected people who came into this country are really, from the point of danger, o bagatelle compared with the amount of contagious disease which we, as a parliament and as a civilization, permit to stalk broadcast through the land. I do not think there is any medical man in this House who will question that. I may say that it is a popular thing, perhaps, in the United States, as it is here, for lion, gentlemen in parliament to make a loud outcry against the possibility of the importation of disease from foreign countries. It is a very popular thing, but I submit that the medical associations of this country are probably the bodies best qualified to judge of what the



danger to Canada is from the importation -of disease from outside, and I do not think that up to this time the Department of Agriculture and tlie Department of the Interior have had any very strong recommendations from the medical bodies of Canada on this point. I speak, of course, subject to correction, but I again assert that we permit year after year loathsome and contagious diseases to be propagated in this country, and we have not the courage to take measures to prevent it.
Mr. CDSiLER. The doctor has touched on a very delicate subject. He refers to the diseases which have been a curse to civilization as far back as civilization goes. He, as a member of the medical profession, and all of his brothers, are unable to suggest any remedy for these diseases, and although he makes the accusation that we in this parliament are making a loud outcry about a small number of contagious cases, whether they are from the outside or not, I do not tnink that he will take the responsibility of bringing a law into this House to check the evil to which he refers, bad enough as it is. But that does not prevent us from doing what we can to prevent an evil which is checkable. The other is not checkable, in so far as civilization has not been able to suggest a remedy, but we are dealing with something which is checkable ; and if he, as a physician, says that the fact that 080 persons suffering from dangerous and contagious diseases have been refused admission to the United States is something that does not affect Canada, I think he is making a mistake. That is a statement that laymen will not agree with, no matter how much doctors may endorse it.
I did not say that certain cases should not be kept out. I do not wish to toe misunderstood in that.
The hon. member said that this was simply a bagatelle, and that I was talking trash.
I said it was a bagatelle compared with the great evils that are stalking unchecked through the country.

May I suggest to the hon. gentleman, as a member of the very honourable profession of medicine, that he take it up and bring in a measure to check the evil resulting from the diseases to which he refers ?

I admit that I have not the courage to deal with some of the evils to which he has referred, some that probably will not be mentioned, but take the case of consumption, of tuberculosis-we have not the courage to deal with it, and it is a disease which is a hundred times more important to the health of Canada than any of the ordinary contagious diseases that we refuse entrance to at the ports.

I am not a member of the Agricultural Committee, and I understand Mr. KENDALL
that committee has been gathering a good deal of information regarding the immigration of the past year. As the report of that committee is not available to us, I will have to ask the minister for some information. I find in the report of the deputy minister the following short paragraphs
In connection with the work of the department in the old country, it may be interesting to note that all booking agents represent the department and are -paid seven shillings for each whole -ticket and a half of that amount for half tickets on all agricultural settlers coming to Canada.
In addition to this the department has a large number of local agents, most of whom are booking agents. They are paid at the rate of twelve shillings for each whole ticket, and half that amount for half tickets on all agricultural settlers.
From that statement it is evident that we pay to the agents a fee for every agricultural settler that leaves Britain for Canada. If that is the case I suppose there must be receipts for the payment and tabulated statements of the number we pay for, and consequently the number that come to settle in. Canada. Can the minister give us that statement ?

I wish to refer to the statement of the member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) and more especially because lie is a medical man who would be expected to appreciate at its full value what it means to import diseased individuals into Canada and scatter them throughout the country. The hon. gentleman state-d that the number of diseased immigrants was a mere bagatelle compared with the total, but wbeu we know that one diseased person may affect 125 or 175 persons, we ought to be able to appreciate what it means to import contagious or infectious disease. Tlie report of tiie chief commissioner of immigration for tlie United-States, tells us that in 1903 they deported at the Canadian line no less than 1,439 immigrants who were affected with contagious and infectious diseases.
What were they ?

It does not specify the disease, but it says they were dangerous and contagious diseases, and that is sufficient for a medical man to understand the danger. Now, as the Americans deported 1,439 to -Canada, and as we sent back to Europe and the continent only 300. it stands to reason that over 1,100 are left iu Canada suffering from dangerous contagious diseases. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Kendall) says that you do not hear the medical men complaining about this ; but lie must have been in the House last year or the year before when an eminent medical man from Montreal drew attention to the fact that many of these diseased persons were drifting into the hospitals and into the thickly populated portions of the community, and that they were also found in the country places

amongst farmers. For three years in succession attention has been drawn to this in the House, and each year the government state that it is exercising every vigilance. This year the Minister of the Interior says he has commenced to take precautions, but last year and the year before he said t'ke same thing. The minister has told us that in the present state of the law he cannot interfere with immigrants coming into Canada if they are cot diseased, but who might be otherwise undesirable. Well, it is the minister and his supporters, and not the opposition, who have ilie power to change the law to make it effective, and why do they not do so ? I believe there is great room for improvement in our quarantine regulations. I have noticed that* in Ontario a very common disease is trachoma or granular eyelids, which is regarded as very contagious when chronic, and patients suffering from it have been admitted into the hospitals at Toronto and at Montreal. Does that not verify the statement made by the American Commissioner of Ini migration, that whereas they have turned back 1,439 diseased persons to Canada. we have sent back only 300 ?
Were these all trachoma?
I do not know and I do not care so long as the disease is dangerous and contagious.

Does the hon. gentleman not know that in a shipload of immigrants with a few cases of trachoma on board, the disease might spread and not show for some days after the immigrants were landed fcere% How could the medical inspector turn such people back ?

There is no doubt the disease might spread on shipboard, but it would only be a few days until it would become evident, and any intelligent medical man could recognize it. If he found one case of trachoma he would know the others who associated with the sufferer and continuing in his inquiry any intelligent medical man could tell very readily what the nature of the disease was. That being so, caution s'hould be exercised to prevent these people going through the country and mixing with other people. All who are brought here are not quarantined. Some are kept for a short time for treatment, and then allowed to go. But there is that undeniable fact, that many must be in the country somewhere, and to that extent the quarantine efforts of the department are a failure.

Will the hon. gentleman answer me this question ? Is it within human power, unless a whole shipload of immigrants are quarantined for a certain length of time, for any medical man to sav that a certain number will not develop the disease after they leave the ship ?
That might happen.
It might not only happen, but it has happened again and again.

When are these people examined ? They are all examined at once when they cross the line; and yet 1,400 have been sent back by the American quarantine officers. Surely our Canadian professional men are as intelligent and can detect the disease as readily as the Americans. There are undoubtedly many other cases in the incipient stages of the disease which are not detected by the American officers, and these would add to the number for the year. The fact that our inspectors did not send these cases back suggests to me that our Canadian regulations are not as strictly enforced as they should be. I want to say a word or two with regard to the other immigration that has been coming in of late ; I notice that our country of late years has been overrun with a large number of people whom I regard as undesirable immigrants. I do not know whether they are Russian Jews or Italians or what they are, but you will find them wherever you go throughout the country. Only two weeks ago, when I was at home, I made a trip of about twenty miles, and in that distance I met no less than half a dozen of these men whom I call Russian Jews, pedlars with packs on their backs, some of them lying and resting in fence corners. I do not say that these are the worst class, because they are not as bad as diseased people ; but to my mind they are not a very desirable class. They do not enter into the industrial activities of the country. It is true, they carry on a trade, a sort of Jew trade. I sometimes think they may be allied with others and have something to do with the robberies that occur from time to time. They go into houses and ply their trade with an assiduity which is peculiar only to themselves. They are a filthy-looking class of people. In summer they may be seen in every direction ; in winter they are 'found around hotels and railway stations plying their trade. They are not the class of people likely to elevate the society or the civilization of the Canadian people, and they are not likely to assimilate with our people to any advantage.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What would my hon. friend suggest to prevent them coming in ?

I would suggest a stricter regulation at the frontier, the same as the Americans have ; if necessary, I would put a poll-tax on every one of them; and I would deport those who are likely to become a charge on the charity of the people as soon as they land. There is no reason why we should be obliged! to accept the riff-raff of every other country in the world, and tax I the charity and generosity of our people to ! maintain not only those who have moderate

730C
health. but those who are affected with incurable diseases.
Can the minister give me the information I asked for ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We can readily give information as to the number of people to whom we paid bonuses and the places where they were paid. The bonuses are paid to the steamship agents in the British Isles and on the continent of Europe. The statement comes from them to the department here, it is sent to the office at Winnipeg to be checked, it is brought back and adjusted between the department and the office of the steamship company. If my hon. friend would like a statemeiit, I can have it laid on the table to-morrow.

I would like to ask the minister if we are paying for the immigrants who' come in and settle on the lands of the colonization companies. For instance, we are informed that a number have settled on the lands of the Saskatchewan Valley Laud Company. I was told that many of these come in as immigrants for which the agents in the United States were paid $3 a piece, and then the land company takes advantage of them, and reports them as having been brought in by themselves ; and for that the land is given to the colonization company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The only check we have upon the people who come in and are reported by our agents as having been sent through their efforts, is the fact that the agent gives a certificate to the intending immigrant, and upon that certificate the bonus is paid. That is checked by our inspector." Of course, there is no possible system under which at times we are not liable to be defrauded to some extent. The only thing we can do is to watch the inspection as carefully and closely as we can. There may be a few people to whom the bonuses are paid who are not sent by agents, but they are only a very few.
When are these certificates collected ? Have you not information as to where the person is located ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The certificate given by the agent entitles the intending immigrant to reduced fare. It' is presented to the railway company, which returns it to us, and upon receipt of the certificate the bonus is paid.

Suppose a man in the United States wants to make a trip across the line and go back again, he can get one of these certificates, I should think, without much difficulty. How do you know that there is not one such in every ten you are paying for ?
Are they paid by the Canadian government ?

As far as I can see, the only way they could get paid from the government would be by checking these men through as settlers and through government agents. I do not believe however that they were paid by the Canadian government. I am not going to deal with the question of the difference in the cost of immigration which the taking of this fifty percent off the settler immigration would make. Last year we spent three-quarters of a million dollars on immigration, and if you take the number of immigrants who went on farms and divide that into the amount of dollars, you can say that each immigrant cost so much. And I believe it would be fair and just to cut off fifty per cent of the immigration, which would make the average cost of each' immigrant considerably higher. But what I want to deal more particularly with is this immigration which is not brought in for farming purposes, but which serves its purpose, and which the labouring men of the country warned the people against, and the labouring men have seen their prophecies fulfilled. I am not going to deal with this question either in opposition to or in favour of the immigration policy in respect to the settlement of land. I appreciate the fact that there is in Canada a scarcity of farm labour, that this question is a large one and growing. and that it looks as if it were going to be more serious in the future. The difficulty so far is one to which we have not attempted to apply any remedy, and the government have settled on no policy as to how we are going to supply the farmers of Canada with labour by the month or the year. I believe we have not properly started on that problem yet, and it is a serious one. But what I want to point,out is that the wage-workers, the city workers, should not be expected to bear the whole brunt of carrying labour on the labour market for nine months in order that the farmer may use it for two or three months. There is this practice in vogue in Canada among the majority of farmers. In Ontario it is used to a considerable extent and in the west to a large extent. Our farmers require labour just in about the same proportion as they require binders. They require it just when their crops are ripe. They want it for a
short time and at a reasonable wage for that short time, and then cast it over on the general labour market for the rest of the year. It is not fair, nor is it a solution of the problem, to imagine that by filling the cities with labour for nine months in the year, the farmer can get relief for two or three months. I am not going to advise the farmer, but if he does not run his business in such a way that he may employ labour all the year round, perhaps he is not managing it as it should be. And it is possible that farms might be run here as they are in other countries, where the farmers can offer employment by the year. Some hon. members, especially from the west, may say that there are positions offered on the farms by the year. No doubt there are, but this, advice is always given to the men : It will be better for you to work by the year at five dollars, eight dollars or ten dollars per month than spend your time during nine months looking for work, and work during a couple of months at $35 or $40 per month. But the question I am dealing with is the question of immigi-ation, which is not settler immigration, and I do not want to mix it up with the other at all. I do not want to exaggerate any condition of affairs, and am not going to rely altogether on my own judgment. I wish however just to read a paragraph from a Winnipeg paper, written just after a large work had been started there a few months ago. It is headed :
' Unskilled Labour Cheap ; common labourers are being paid 15 cents per hour.'
What paper ?
The Winnipeg ' Free Press.'
That is not a good authority.

I am simply quoting nfews matter and not editorial matter.
Common labourers are being paid 15 cents per hour, which is the present rate in the city tor unskilled labour. Some surprise was expressed by the reporter for the ' Free Press ' at the low scale of wages, but the manager of the employment agency said that there was no difficulty in securing Galicians and Hungarians at this figure. On inquiry from other sources this statement was confirmed, as several large employers of rough labour say that they can get any amount of unskilled labour at the price stated. One employer said that this was the lowest rate he had paid in the last three years for the same class of labour.
That gives an idea of the demoralized state of the labour market, so far as the wage-earner is concerned in Winnipeg and the west this year. Fifteen cents an hour for unskilled labour means a drop of 74 cents . and I will risk my word that skilled labour, in most instances, took a corresponding drop. Now, this is a serious thing. The labourer cannot possibly live decently on

what he earns at fifteen cents an hour. It is a serious matter for every wage-earner in the country. And. perhaps, I may be permitted to point out the contrast. When wages are at this low rate it means that all hope of enjoying the prosperity of the cpun-try is gone so far as concerns the man who sells his labour for wages. It was complained all last year, and for some time past in fact, that some people in other countries were-as it is called-dumping goods in Canada. That means, our manufacturers say, that others were actually selling goods to the people of Canada for less than it cost to produce the goods. And this was supposed to be-perhaps was, but I will only say supposed to be, as it is not necessary that I should deal with that question now-a serious state of affairs. That was the manufacturers' complaint. It looked like being an issue in this country. But it was forestalled; it was headed off. We have this session the dumping clause and we are told by the Minister of Finance that it is one of the most radical propositions ever adopted by any parliament, and that this government and this parliament are leading the way. But the case here is worse than dumping, for dumping is sending goods into this country and selling them here at less than it costs to produce them. But we are spending hundreds of thousands of dollars of public money every year, and other parties in this country are spending many thousands of dollars of money that does not belong to the government to bring in Canada, not farm settlers, but skilled workmen and labourers of all kinds to depress and break down the labour market in Canada. Is that fair to the worker ? We declare that our principle in Canada is protection. Protection indeed
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Puttee) is mistaken. Skilled labour is scarce in Canada.
Who advises that ?

That is published by ' Yours faithfully, Canadian Labour Bureau, Louis Leopold, Secretary.' This matter was brought strikingly to my attention the last time I was in Winnipeg. The fact is I could not stay in the office and attend to anything I wanted to do by reason of the men who came in in numbers showing me the guarantees issued by this Leopold. And these same guarantees of employment have some bearing on the question, which I will deal with later on, as to who it is that wants these men. Here is one of these guarantees which was given to me by one of the men who brought it out from Eng land. It is headed ' Canadian Labour Bu reau ' and then comes the coat of arms of Canada :
13 Charing Cross, London, S.W.,
8th April, 1904.
My dear Sir,-This will serve to introduce to you Mr. W. J. Boorn who is proceeding to *Winnipeg with a view to taking employment as a carpenter. I shall be grateful if you will advise him in his best interests and if you will give him suitable work, or if you will address him to a firm who are in need of his class of help. I beg to commend him to your kind consideration and to thank you in anticipation for anything you may do on his behalf.
I am, dear, sir,
Yours faithfully,
Canadian Labour Bureau, LOUIS LEOPOLD, Secretary.
The President,
The Manitoba Construction Co., Madomock Block, Port St.,
Winnipeg.
That was brought to me soon after it had been presented to the foreman of the construction company, and the foreman told the man who delivered this, that there had been 150 of them there that day, and advised him to go back and sue Louis Leopold for bringing them out under false pretenses. The hon. gentleman asks who he represents. I believe that in this business he represents more particularly the Canadian Manufacturers Association, but financially he represents Louis Leopold himself. He had
reason lately to cause the publication of a letter in Winnipeg in which he states :
It may interest the representatives of the Winnipeg Trades and Labour Council to know that the position in this building has added largely to the result of my business, and that the government officials have even tried several times to get me out of it, but have failed, as I have secured the premises on a long lease.
This agency is in the same building as the Canadian government agency, and he boasts here that this brought him a great deal of business, though he says that the Canadian government cannot get him out. But the point I am trying to drive home is that when it comes to the manufacturer asking for anything we can take such radical steps, but when it comes to the workingmen asking for anything, the furthest we can go is to put an advertisement in the English papers saying that we are not responsible for this man's doings.
