I think that the authorities should find some effective means of stopping this matter where it is now. I brought the same matter up last year ; if it had been effectively dealt with then we would not have been overrun, as we have been overrun, with a lot df deluded mechanic immigrants this year. I have here the prospectus of this Louis Leopold Company, and'I have a tremendous list that was sent over of so-called vacancies in Canada-list after list, giving the number, not only in each trade but in each particular branch. There are also a number of letters that have been sent to me by men to whom Louis Leopold gave them, sending them to various members of the Manufacturers Association asking for work. The Manufacturers Association of course is the body that asks for 25,000 workingmen. I have here a bunch of these recommendations, and every one of them is addressed to a concern in this country that had a strike on at the time. Why, under this same rule it would be just as well if the Sydney Steel Works were to telegraph over to Britain now that they wanted 2,000 men in Sydney right away, that business was so pressing that they wanted the men. Of course they have locked out their men, and so have these other concerns to whom recommendations are sent. In view of this list of vacancies, I may mention that in to-days papers there is a further statement from the Canadian Manufacturers Association in which they claim that over 7,000 vacancies are existing now, giving the numbers, province by province, and in some cases the- trades are given. That is the kind of statement that leads people who are not working for wages and who are not in touch with those that are, to imagine that there is a scarcity of skilled workmen in Canada to-day. If that statement to-day is honest and fair, I say that the one of last year was not, and I do not believe that this one is either. If it is, 1 if their intentions are right, instead of say-
What do you mean ?

That he is made an agent of the Immigration Department for the sake of recommending Canada and selling tickets to Canada rather than to other countries. I notice, for instance, that the commissioner over there, Mr. Preston, recognizes it; in fact I imagine that there has been trouble there, he evidently recognizes that there might be, though he states the contrary. He says :
Very many of the booking agents on account of this financial advantage accruing to them, were believed able to exert some influence in cultivating public opinion in their own localities in favour of the Dominion. In doing so, even if they found such a course financially advantageous, they have not been guilty of conduct which any business man has the slightest occasion to be ashamed of.
I draw the inference that there have been some pretty shady dealings with ticket agents using the stationery of the Dominion government. It may be said to be necessary for Mr. Preston to appoint ticket agents in Great Britain to be immigration agent so that they could put in a good word for Canada when the undecided immigrant comes along, but see how it connects the department generally with this mechanic immigration which has been coming out. Here is a bill that was given to me by a man who brought it in his pocket believing that its presentation would give him work at 55 cents an hour. It is headed :

speechtext: What is the date ?	.

speechtext:
It would be published in the spring. Its last quotation is dated January 1, 1904. From what I know of the conditions of the building trades in Canada,
I would say that the tremendous difference between the building trades in a Canadian city and the building trades in the cities where the men are to whom these circulars are sent out ought to be pointed out. I know a great many men who have worked in the west, in Winnipeg, for twenty years in the building trade who have their records showing what their incomes have been and I am assured by them that in years gone by their records show that the actual number of working days only averaged from 114 to

135 iu the j'ear. The Britisher knows nothing about this. It is hardly one day in three. Even at $5 a day it gives a man an income of about $050 a year, not an extravagant income, but to state the fact that the building trades are so highly paid in Canada and to put it before the mechanic in the old country without any explanation and with the seal and endorsement of the Canadian government misleads. This circular proceeds :
Statement by the Government Emigration Commissioner.

subtopic: CANADA WANTS MORE MEN IN THE BUILDING TRADES.
speechtext: we have had large Immigration expenditures for many years we have reduced them during some years and there did not seem to be very much difference in the results in those years and I am bound to say that the conditions existing in other countries have as much as anything else to do with the settlement of our lands. I do not for one moment interpose any objection to having agents in other countries publishing and distributing authentic information, or to have agents looking after the interests of the country, but it looks to me to be a dangerous thing to have so many agents in other countries often idle hands as they have proved to be. I draw the attention of the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) to some statements which appear in the last printed report of the United States Commissioner General of Immigration ; and perhaps he will not treat these stateihents as flippantly and as lightly as he did the statements made by my colleague as to the quality of some of our immigrants. At page 40 of the last printed report of the United States Commissioner General of Immigration you will find this statement:
In the year 1903 the number of officers engaged in preventing these undesirable immigrants from entering the United States from Canada was increased from 66 to 116.
It was found necessary, in order to preserve the United States from the undesirable immigrants from Canada, to increase the number of officers to that extent. The report says, at page 46 :
During the twelve months ended to-day many persons have applied for admission to the United States via Canada whose personal appearance and ceneral conditions shoull have precluded the possibility of their having been allowed to embark on any vessel designed to carry passengers under conditions of health and comfort.
It is only necessary to relate that in some instances the filthy conditions have been so abominable as to render it impossible for our medical examiners to give them the attention required by our laws and regulations. The Bureau, like myself, will have to leave it to conjecture how fellow passengers huddled together in the close quarters of an Atlantic liner have endured the contaminating presence of such persons.
Mr. PL'TTEE.
Admission to the United States has been invariably denied to such applicants and in some instances it has been deemed unwise to return them to Canada, and deportation to Europe has been effected.
These immigrants were so bad that the United States officers feared to send them back to Canada, because, I presume, they would make attempts to re-enter, and so they shipped them home via New York. The report further says, at page 48 :
Covering a direct line of more than 4,000 miles of frontier including three ocean ports, and inspecting more than 100 trains daily and a large number of ferries, * sound steamers,' and the growing fleets that ply the Great Lakes, these inspectors, in all kinds of inclement weather, and frequently under most trying circumstances, have boarded every train, met every ferry and every steamer, Whether iby riven, lake or sound, and have prevented the amazing total of 5,158 diseased and otherwise objectionable aliens entering the United States, and have done all this without causing a single complaint on the part of the travelling public.
Then follows a tabulated statement of the number of arrests made along the border of persons trying to smuggle undesirable immigrants into the United States. Year after year we on this side of the House have told the Minister of the Interior that we are prepared to assist him in making a reasonable appropriation to ensure a more-efficient medical inspection than that which takes place at the present time. How is it possible that hundreds and hundreds of immigrants who reach Montreal from St John or Halifax are so diseased as not to be admissible to the United States, if a right medical examination was made at the port of landing ? How is it possible that such immigrants are allowed to land at Quebec and Montreal ? What we demand is a more rigid medical examination. These immigrants should not be permitted to embark on the other side of the Atlantic, but if they contract disease on the voyage they should De sent back at the expense of the steamship companies which bring them out. If the statements of the United States officers are reliable, such immigrants should be rigorously kept ojit of Canada. It is extraordinary that we should have the opposition and criticism of hon. gentlemen opposite rather than their sup-port, when we draw the attention of the Minister of the Interior to this matter. We are as anxious as he ought to be to secure eligible immigrants, but we enter our emphatic protest against the laxity of the system which permits hundreds and hundreds of immigrants to remain here who are excluded from the United States. We have just as skilled medical men in Canada as they have in the United States, and' if they are able to successfully grapple with the difficulty, so should we. I believe that in some cases the United States employ Canadian medical officers, which is a compliment to our professional men, and if that ho so, we certainly should have no difficulty

ourselves in finding a sufficient number of suitable inspectors to protect our frontier and ocean ports against the incursion of these immigrants. My bon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson) drew attention to the conditions prevailing in Montreal last spring, when thousands of destitute Italians were permitted to come into this country, and we have not so far been able to place the responsibility for their admission. Some of these poor immigrants became a charge upon the good people of Montreal. The Minister of Labour did not know whence they came. He sent his deputy, a very able and a very clever man, to make inquiries, but he gave it up as a bad job ; and now we have an investigation going on by one of our county judges. Surely there must be something wrong in the machinery of the Labour and Immigration Departments when this untoward condition of things is allowed to go on. We have to call in one of our judges to ascertain where these people came from, under what conditions they werei brought to the country, and what has become of them. It is certainly a very serious problem, and it is our duty to raise our voice in protest on every available occasion, until we are satisfied that the plan of the Minister of the Interior is the most efficient and most rigorous method that can be devised to exclude diseased and undesirable immigrants from Canada. My hon. friehd from Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) has referred to the methods adopted on the other side of the Atlantic to induce people to emigrate to Canada. Last fall, through the co-operation of a friend in England, I secured a large number of circulars issued by Mr. Louis Leopold, advertising situations vacant, &c., and I sent them to the secretary of the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress so that he might see what was going on. My correspondent found the office of Mr. Leopold in the same building as the office of the Canadian immigration agent at London ; he found these circulars bearing the Dominion eoat-of-arins, with the words ' Canadian Labour Bureau ' ; and he found all the surrounding circumstances calculated to mislead the ordinary intending emigrant to believe that if be came to Canada through the instrumentality of this bureau, he was coming under tthe auspices of the Canadian government itself.
As I have said, I gave these documents to the secretary of the Dominion Trades and Labour Council, that he might see for himself what was going on, and take the necessary steps to try to awaken the people of the old country as to the misrepresentations that were being made to induce people to come to this country under the promise that immediate permanent employment could be procured. The last time I was at home I had a visit from a friend of mine, who left me two or three papers which I will take the liberty of reading, and I will then pass
them over to the hon. minister that he may take steps to put a stop to these misrepresentations which are still going on. Three Scotchmen, named Ferris, Brown and Allan, were induced to come to Canada, and were assured of immediate permanent employment at their trade. These men were represented to me to be miners, men who mined the stone of rock surrounding the coal seams. They had splendid letters, I am told, from those by whom they had been employed for many years, and would have made excellent citizens if the representations made to them had been carried out. They were told that if they came to Toronto they could find employment at once. I need not tell the hon. minister that there is no employment for miners in the city of Toronto ; and they looked in vain for work. They were engaged, when my friend called on me a couple of weeks ago, in helping to clear away the debris at the scene of the recent fire. The following letter is to Mr. Ferris :
Canadian Labour Bureau,
Shipping Agency, It Nelson Place, Stirling, 16th April, 1904.
Dear Sir,-I have now pleasure in sending you herewith three boat and rail tickets to Toronto tor yourself, Geo. Brown and John Allan, also a supply of luggage labels for each. Inclosed you will also find two very good letters of introduction, so that you are all sure of employment. You should he ready to embark at Plantation Quay, south side, Glasgow, on 23rd April, at 2 p.m. The balance of the passage money to be paid at 25 Bothwell Street, Glasgow.
Send luggage to reach Glasgow the day before sailing.
I shall he pleased to furnish you with any other information you may desire.
Mr. Ferris was also given a letter by this same Mr. Louis Leopold from the Canadian Labour Bureau, 13 Charing Cross, S. W-
Canadian Labour Bureau,
London, S.W., 14th April, 1904.
My dear Sir,-The bearer of this letter^ is Mr. John Ferris, who Is desirous of getting work in Toronto. He is a brickmaker by trade and X should esteem it a favour If you would advise him as to where he is likely to obtain suitable employment. He is willing to take any work for the time being until he can get a berth in his own line. Thanking you in an-ticioation for anything you may do on his behalf.
I am, dear sir.
Yours faithfully,
Canadian Labour Bureau, LOUIS LEOPOLD,
Secretary.
This letter is addressed to R. J. Younge, Esq.. Canadian Manufacturers Association, Toronto, Canada. Now, Mr. Chairman, there ought to be some means devised to prevent men from being deceived in tills way by agents who represent themselves, and who would appear from the heading on

tlie letter paper, to be agents of the Canadian government. I believe tbe government has recently published in the old country papers an announcement respecting some of these people ; but that to my mind it not sufficient. There ought to be some effort made to secure the co-operation of the imperial authorities to stop this work, which is engaged in. I presume, by those who get a commission from the steamship companies to induce people to come to this country. These men, I believe, two of them at least, are married men who left their families behind them, expecting to bring them out in the fall. They will leave Canada in the *autumn and return home, and they will not act as very earnest advocates of immigration to Canada after their own experience. If this kind of work is permitted to go on unchallenged, a great deal of damage will be done to Canada. As the hon. member for Winnipeg has said, many misrepresentations have been made to induce mechanics to copie to this country. These men have not been able in many cases to get the employment or the wage they were told they could get, and many of them have become dissatisfied and are writing to their friends in the old country denouncing the misrepresentations under which t'hev were induced to come to this country. This is no doubt a difficult matter to deal with, but I do not think we on this side of the House would be doing our duty if we did not point out to the minister the conditions that exist, and I can assure him that he will have our co-operation in any steps he takes to put a stop to a condition of things that is most disgraceful. The effort made by the Department of Labour to keep people from coming in here cannot be regarded as successful. Apparently the machinery used by the Minister of the Interior is not all that it ought to_ be. We are ready to assist him in perfecting that machinery, because we believe it needs perfecting, and in applying the precautions that ought to be taken. The number of immigrants may be somewhat smaller in years to come, but a better class of people will come to our shores, and the result on the whole will be much more beneficial than if the existing condition of things is permitted to continue.

Before the item passes 1 would like to say a word in regard to a matter concerning which I heard some adverse criticism earlier in the day, that is, ns to the measures taken by the Immigration Department during the early spring of this year and the year before to induce a proper class of immigrants to come from Britain. The department sent over last spring and the spring before a number of practical farmers to different parts of the old country for the purpose of inducing a proper class of agricultural immigrants to come to Canada.
I was sorry to hear that system criticised adversely this afternoon. I wish to put on record my view that it is the most effective method which the department has yet adopted for the purpose of inducing a desirable class of British immigrants to come to this country. I think we all agree that the system previously followed of resident agents in the old country was very largely a failure ; and we must admit that the practice of paying a bonus to steamship companies was largely a failure. Both these systems were failures for obvious reasons. I believe that by bringing in contact with the agricultural population of the British islands successful farmers of this country, there is a reasonable probability of securing Mr. SCOTT.
the class of immigrants we most desire. I do not know whether the department intends to continue this system, but I would not like this item to pass, after having heard the somewhat adverse criticisms that were made, without giving my strong endor-sation to that system which has been adopted recently, and which I am satisfied has already been productive of very good results. But still we can reasonably expect that it will be productive of very much better results as time goes on if the system is continued, and as the agricultural population of the old country become more intimately acquainted with the actual farmers who have made a success of farming life in our western country. I do not know but that it would be a good idea to include in these excursions farmers from eastern Canada as well as those from .western Canada ; but. speaking of the west, 1 would certainly, as a western man, wish to endorse most strongly that system of inducing immigration, and I do not consider that the expense so far incurred is at all out of proportion to the benefits likely to accrue ; in fact, I think that a very large part of the money which has been hitherto spent for immigratioi purposes in the old country, both in the employment of permanent agents there and in paying bonuses to steamship companies, was money absolutely thrown away, or worse than thrown away, and that whether this amount that is now spent be large or small it is for a good purpose, and there is every reason to Relieve that it will produce a good result.

Boche) has referred to be a true account of unavoidable circumstances in the North-west, I would take that as a reason why it should not be distributed. From the time I have taken the immigration work under my charge, we have considered that the truth was good enough to be told with regard to the Northwest, and in telling the truth we have succeeded in this at least: that the people to whom we addressed our literature, believe the representations made in it. If I found in a document which my officers thought was desirable literature to be circulated, that the truth was told as to a storm or anything of that kind, I am not at all sure I would (have rejected it simply because that which happens in every agricultural country was shown to have happened in Northwestern Canada. I can express no opinion about it; it was not my own personal act. but I venture the statement that the people who read that paper were not prejudiced against Canada, by reason of that statement, because any one who knows anything about agriculture in all countries, knows that conditions of this kind arise at times. I have been asked for an explanation and that is the only explanation I can give.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) referred at some length to a number of things which have been explained before and in respect to which the position of the government has remained absolutely clear, and it seems like foolish repetition to keep repeating the same explanation over and over again. However, inasmuch as my hon. friend (Mr. Puttee) has the appearance and earnestness in urging some of these points, perhaps I might say a word in regard to them. So far as his statement is concerned, that the labour market in Winnipeg is in such a state that ordinary unskilled labour is bringing only fifteen cents per hour, I say at once that I positively refuse to accept that statement as being a correct description of the labour market in Winnipeg. I do not think it is correct, and I will require more evidence than the hon. gentleman's remarks before I accept it as correct. I was in Winnipeg before my hon. friend (Mr. Puttee) represented that city, and I have seen the workingmen of that city packing their grips and travelling out because there were no people coming in ; because the country which is tributary to Winnipeg and of which Winnipeg is the entrepot, was not being settled up. I can tell my hon. friend that the reason why this $6,000,000 worth of buildings is going up in the city of Winnipeg now is because of the successful immigration policy carried on under this government. If my hon. friend's constituents are prosper-

ous and if the city he represents is prosperous, it is the immigration policy which j my hon. friend has done his best to prevent and discourage which is largely responsible for that prosperity. With regard to the point to which attention has been drawn at great length, respecting the misrepresentations which have been made in the old country, I can only say that that is one of the things which is going to take place under any system of encouraging the immigration of agriculturists. No one ever saw an army without camp followers, and no one ever saw a great movement of population without a certain residium following it, and certain things happening as a consequence of the movement having been inaugurated. It is quite true that certain persons have taken advantage of the immigration movement from Great Britain to Canada, of the advertising we have done, and of the dissemination of information which has taken place under this department, for the purpose of making money in a cheap and easy way by making false representations to mechanics and other people in order to induce them to come to Canada. But the government of Canada is not responsible for that, and I repudiate any responsibility for any false representations made by any one in the United Kingdom. Until this parliament assumes the responsibility of placing on the statute-book a law to enable us to deal with cases of that kind-and I doubt the possibility of parliament placing any such law on the statute-book-I am not disposed to hold myself responsible for anything done in that way. As to the labour bureau setting itself up and making false representations as to the condition of the people in Canada, that is the responsibility of the people making them. We have no law whereby we can prevent any person who sees fit to place a heading on his letter paper which leads an uneducated person to suppose that he is, an agent of the Canadian government. We have no law by which we can prevent or punish him. That which we can do we have done. We have sent to a large number of the British newspapers a distinct statement warning the public that the people who are making these representations are not authorized agents of the Canadian government. We have endeavoured to get rid of that office in Charing Cross, but so far without success.

I want to say a word or two with regard to the subject of medical inspection. From the time Dr. Bryce took charge,
I think I can say the inspection became effective. The changes which he brought about became effective about the 1st of April, and since that time I think the medical inspection has been as effective as it can be made. I cannot imagine any way in which it could be made more effective. If my lion friends will take the trouble to go and see the method by which this inspection is carried on, they will be satisfied that the fault does not rest with our officials at the present time. In the first place, we have an inspection for quarantine purposes conducted by the Department of Agriculture. We do not depend on that at all, because the quarantinable diseases do not include all the diseases of an infectious or loathsome character. At the port of Quebec, for instance, the immigrants are landed on the dock, and are sent to a passage way in a building and are ranged off in such a way that they cannot get away. They are brought through a narrow passage which leads through a turnstile into the room where the doctor is waiting to inspect them. There the examination is made and the immigrant has to pass inspection to the satisfaction of the doctor. There is only one possible way in which the inspection can fail to be effective, and that is if the doctor is incompetent ; and as the agent and officers of the department are present and take charge of the immigrants as they are put through the inspection, it is next to Impossible that the doctor could be incompetent without some one being aware of the fact. During a short visit I paid to the station at Quebec, no less than -2 400 people passed through the hands of the inspector during that day. In the twenty-four hours there were no less than three steamers arrived loaded with immigrants. It is possible Mr. SIFTON.
of course that two or three or a half a dozen of this large number might have got through who were affected, not with any serious disease, but with some skin disease of an apparently trifling character ; but taken on the whole, we have a system which I think is effective. I fully recognize the paramount importance of making whatever system we mav adopt as effective as possible.
I want to add further this remark, that I think my hon. friend, after a little reflection, will admit that no matter what kind of inspection we may have in Canada at the seaboard and all along the border-of course we have none at present along the border, and that would be a very large question of policy to consider-you would still have large numbers of people rejected by the American inspectors as unfit to enter the United States. Take the case at Sault Ste. Marie. For years people have been coming across from northern Michigan in small groups to work in the woods where pulp-wood is taken out. Many of these people are Canadians who had gone to Michigan and who were returning from that state. When the lumber mills were closed in Michigan for lack of logs, a considerable number of people who had been engaged in that business crossed our border ; and when the time came when many of them wanted to go back, the Americans had established a most rigid system of inspection at the Sault. Under that system many of the people were prevented going back. Our agent tlieie told me personally, in answer to an inquiry regarding the number of people who had been stopped there, that the excuses under which people were rejected by the American inspectors were in many cases absolutely ridiculous. One man was rejected on the ground of deformity, simply because he had one-Iialf an inch taken off one of ins fingers, and that man had come in from the United States in that condition. These inspectors placed along the line will find excuses for rejecting a considerable number of people, and however thorough our system of inspection may be, there will be more or less of that sort "of thing all the time.

The crops of this eastern part of Saskatchewan have been good and better, never good and poor-the old settlers say they have never kno-wn a failure ; last year and this year have shown very fine crops, both in quantity and quality.
And he underlines this :
The usual drawbacks occur, danger from frost, drought, small yield from poor farming, from gophers, bad effects of weeds.
But lie leaves out the following :
But in no part of the Northwest, and therefore In no part of Canada Is a yearly crop 'Of wheat, oat, barley or flax more assured than in the Saskatoon district.
The hon. gentleman has picked out a little piece in the middle where the writer says there are the usual drawbacks, such as are to be found in any country. But, taking the whole article I think it is a very fair one. I would not object to it going out. It is written about a part of my constituency, and I have no objection to it whatever. I believe in telling the truth about these matters.

is running down their country. How much did these American immigrants get for their land before they came to Canada ? According to that newspaper cut, land there is worth from $75 to $100 an acre. That is the effect of high protection.

Surely the hon. gentleman does not say that it is high protection that has made the land worth $75 an acre. High protection has not made land worth $75 an acre. If high protection made land dear, it is strange that in 1896 farm lands in Ontario had gone down so far that you could'nt sell them for enough to pay the mortgage. That is a false statement, and you know it.

I will venture to say that in the constituency which the hon. membe'' for Compton (Mr. Pope) represents there were a great many houses with slats on the windows in 1896.	.
That is the old story repeated by the Minister of Agriculture fifteen years ago. You ought to get somebody else to post you.

A lot of people were living in houses that were nailed up with slabs, because they were so poor that they could not buy window glass. Is there anything wrong in saying that we have millions of acres of land to give away free to settlers in the Northwest ? It says that settlers' effects are brought in duty free. Anything wrong about that ?
Is that new ?
Is there any reason for concealing it, because it is not new ? Did you do it in 1896 ?
Yes.

When you brought over Jew pedlars that we had to arrest in the Northwest Territories and put into jail ? I heard some gentleman complain about the miserable class of immigrants we are getting at present. When the hon. gentleman's friends were running the immigration machine they spent a great deal of money and got very little results. The immigrants were like gophers, dodging into one hole and dodging out of another ; they came in on one train
and out on another. They said they brought in 16,000 immigrants in one year ; but if they did, I venture to say there were 25,000 went out-the census shows that.	The census shows that in a certain number of years they were supposed to bring into this country something like' 1,000,000 people, and they got the money to do it with, but when the census was taken all these people had evaporated, and the natural increase had gone as well.
Because the hon. gentleman and his friends were telling the world that this country was not fit to live in.

The member for Marquette is doing the same thing at present ; he is putting on ' Hansard ' a matter to show that the country is no good. To show how far afield the hon. member for Marquette had to go, how hard pressed he was for something to say against the government, he selected out of a whole page one line and garbled it to bring an accusation against the government. He read this paragraph :
There was very little number 1 hard in 1902, and while the prospects for this grade were good a few weeks ago, as a result of the big storm

He underlines these words, ' As a result of the big storm.'
-there will be not much more this year, or in other words, the grades will compare equally for the two years.
If there had not been a big storm I do not know what the hon. gentleman would have done for some ground on which to criticise the immigration department. Everybody knew there was a storm last year, and that it reduced the grade of wheat. It was no use for the hon. gentleman to try to hide that when we had thousands of people travelling all over the country examining it and writing to their friends in the United States. One of the reasons for which the minister has been so successful is in the character of the immigration literature. In all the immigration literature that has been circulated by this government in the last five or six years there has been a fair statement of the conditions which we have in this country. People do not come in under false pretenses, they know the length of the winter, they know we have good seasons and occasionally we have bad seasons, and when they come they find that we have given them nothing but facts. The fact that we had 125,000 immigrants last year shows that our immigration literature has borne good fruit. These people who came in last year do not come empty-handed ; whereas, in 1896. the hon. gentlemen opposite brought in people that had not much money. These people who came in last year brought in six or seven million dollars in cash or goods. They also brought in with them a lot of money of which we have no account at all. I suppose when the immigration officials ask

a man how much money he has got, he says I have $100, $200 or $300. That is the record that the Minister of the Interior gets. But when a gentleman comes into that country with $300 in his pocket, he looks over the country, he makes up his mind that it is a good country to settle in, and he immediately writes back to his agents and tells them to sell out his holdings. Those are sold for $6,000 or $7,000, and that money is all sent across the border and deposited in a Cana dian bank, but the Minister of the Interior lias no record of that at all. So it is impossible for us to arrive at an estimate of the amount of money these people have brought in. The manager of the Union Bank at Saskatoon told me that when he opened business there the head office instructed him to be very careful about making loans, told him to keep his loans inside his deposits. He started out with the idea that he was not going to do much business but he was not there one month until he could not loan out half the money he was getting in on deposit from these people that were coming into the country. I say that to-day we have a record of some $6,000,000 or $7,000,000 these people have brought in. but they have brought in millions more besides. A lot of wealthy people came in from the United 'States. Hon. gentlemen talk about the vast public debt, some $35 per capita. Now, every one of these 125,000 is helping to reduce that debt, they are all taking a share of it on their shoulders. In bringing in 125,000 people you bring in six millions of money, and you get all that by an expenditure of $650,000 on immigration. I think it is pretty good business, and if the minister keeps on the people of this country will be pretty well satisfied.

I am sure the Minister of the Interior will be grateful to the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) for coming to his rescue in defence of the campaign literature that he is circulating under the guise of immigration literature. I do not know whether the literature my hon. friend has read is correct or not, but I think it is fair to say that it is not in the best interests of the people of Canada. We complain that the Minister of the Interior selects the leading political journal of his province and pays out of the public treasury $7,500 to circulate it under the guise of immigration literature for the purpose of inducing people to come to.Canada. I have no time at this late hour to enter into a discussion of the matter contained here. The hon. member for Saskatchewan has gone over this paper very minutely this evening, and I do not intend to follow his example, but I will just produce one illustration. I have here some reports of the farm delegates that were sent to the old country by the hon. Minister of the Interior last year for the purpose of telling the people there of the grandeur of the Northwest of Canada. One of these gentlemen has made a reference to this kind of eam-Mr. DAVIS.
paign literature, find perhaps he would be a good authority. Mr. W. H. Bryce, who was one of the farm delegates selected by this government, says :
The information that is given in the literature that is distributed is not what the people want. They do not believe what is printed.
That is what this gentleman says about this kind of literature. I repeat the statement that I think the hon. minister should consider the expenditure of money a little more carefully. I say that it will always be open for discussion and that some portion of the Canadian people will have some right to condemn the hon. gentleman if he is going to subsidize one of the leading political organs in his own province for the purpose of inducing old country people to come to Canada.
I want to say one or two words in respect to the old country delegates, and if it is the policy of this government to continue sending successful farmers from the Northwest to the old country I would like to direct the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that there was practically no preparation for these gentlemen when they arrived in Great Britain. Thomson, delegate-to Scotland says :

Here is a delegate who was sent to the old country. There was no preparation made for this gentleman and he asks that some preparation should be made so that the delegate could go to work immediately without travelling hither and thither in the old country. Another gentleman, Mr. H. C. Whellams, in his report to the government, says :
On the third of March I went to Gloucester, and I was at first somewhat disappointed to find no advertising done'. I at once arranged with the papers for a thorough and complete system of posting and advertising through the columns of the local papers, also by means of hand bills posted throughout the country.
Here is a gentleman sent to the old country to tell the people about the Northwest and when he arrives at his destination he finds that no advertising has been done. Nobody knows that he is in the old country at all. He makes this complaint in his report to the government. Mr. Hugh Mc-Gillivray another of these delegates says :
I started at Aylesbury, the county town, and visited all the principal towns, taking a town each day on market days. I advertised in the local papers ahead and on my arrival would put

These are some of the points that I W'ould bring to the attention of the hon. minister if it is the policy of the government to continue sending these gentlemen to the old country. I am sure it cannot be said that we are not spending enough money on Mr. Preston and his colleagues in the old country. Surely these gentlemen would have an opportunity of making some preparation for the delegates that we sent over there and who cost the people of Canada $25,000. How did the hon. gentlemen, expect that they would find these delegates when they only remained in these towns from one to two days ?
I would like to ask the hon. minister what the policy of the government is in respect to the scarcity of farm hands in Ontario and eastern Canada or if the government has any policy upon that question. Is the hon. gentleman going to give that question any consideration or not and does he propose putting any amount in the estimates so that the people of Ontario and eastern Canada may be better supplied with farm hands ? I did hear the hon. gentleman make the statement that there was no complaint of that kind made during last year. The hon. gentleman has been misinformed because several complaints have been made and the complaint I think is as great as ever it was in the central part of Ontario and in Quebec. Yet the hon. gentleman seems to give it no attention. In view of the fact that this condition has existed for so many years and that there has been coming to the government year after year a universal complaint that farm hands in Ontario and the eastern part of Chnada were scarce, it is time that the hon. gentleman gave some attention to *this question so that the farmers of eastern *Canada might derive some advantage from the very large expenditure of money that is being made for immigration.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have been giving the subject attention for the last two years. We sent some thousands of labourers to the province of Ontario who were distributed amongst the farmers in that province. I am informed that a very considerable number have gone this year. I am quite satisfied that a larger number could have been absorbed and profitably placed in the province of Ontario if a more effective system of distribution were adopted. There is a system of distribution through the officers of the government of Ontario centralized at Toronto. In my judgment a thoroughly effective system of distribution for Quebec and Ontario would be' to provide agents at the port of debarkation so that the labourers would be taken charge of when they landed at Quebec and distributed from there to the point where they were to be employed. I am giving that my attention and I hope with the cooperation of the governments of Ontario and Quebec to adopt a system that will be effective.
I am bound to say that a great deal of caution is necessary in dealing with a subject of that kind. It would be very undesirable for the depai-tment to dump a large number of labourers either in Ontario or Quebec and find that the system of distributing them was not effective so that a considerable number of them were left without employment. We could not take a risk like that, we have to consider a variety of things such as the housing of the labourers while they are getting employment, and in Quebec and Ontario these present a good deal of difficulty. We have our establishment at Winnipeg and the people there have got into the habit of sending to the provincial and Dominion agents so that the resu't is that the work of the two governments together results in a very effective system of distribution. Both last year and this year we have sent a very large number of labourers and have supplied a very pressing demand, and we hope to be able to make it more effective as time goes on.

In our section of the province of Quebec we have received kind consideration from ilr. Marquette, the provincial immigration agent at Montreal, but we have not been able to get the number of labourers we require. In eastern Canada we can utilize not only immigrants who are suitable as farm labourers, but our industrial development there is capable of employing many who would not be suitable in the' west, i f it were arranged that the public who desire servants would know where to apply for them, they would very soon all be placed. We have this advantage, that one or two years training on a farm in eastern Canada, would be very useful for these people if jthey should afterwards go west. Our farmers' sons are rapidly going to the west, and the farmers find themselves short of labour. There is thus an opportunity of developing the usefulness of these immigrants as suitable settlers in the west.

Mr. OLIVER, No, I do not say that. I am not responsible for what this writer heard.

No, I won't. I would not be so foolish as to contradict every idiotic rumour a man may hear.' The district of Alberta is not in need of defence against absurd rumours. If it would be a crime against this country, had these statements appeared in the ' Free Press,' supposing they had been as the hon. member for Marquette said, how much greater crime it was against this country, against the district of Saskatchewan and the district of Alberta, that these statements should be embodied in ' Hansard,' and become a part of the permanent records of this country, as they have been as the result of the hon. member's efforts. If the facts were -as the 'hon.. member for King's said they were, Iwhen they were not, then he committed a (greater offence against the welfare of this (country than the man who wrote them or the man who published the paper, because he made them a part of the official record of this country on his responsibility as a member of parliament.
Mr. FOWLER, I would very much prefer being accused of lack of mentality than to be proved out of my own mouth of an absolute lack of honesty and lack of candour, and that is the position which the just now ferocious member for Alberta occupies be-lore this House. The hon. gentleman listened to-night to an attack by one of his colleagues on the district he represents, and he sat there dumb as an oyster apparently not daring to open his mouth ; and when I challenge the hon. gentleman to stand up in his place and defend the district from which he comes, he tries to draw a herring across the trail and accuses the hon. member for Marquette of defaming the Northwest when the hon. gentleman for Marquette very properly drew the attention of this House to the fact that this government was spending over $7,000 of public money to disseminate in tne United States absolute libels and falsehoods respecting the country.
The hon. member for Marquette did not say they were libels. He said they were probably true, but they should not be circulated.

The hon. gentleman for Marquette did characterize them as libels. He drew the attention of the House to the publication of that sheet for the purpose of showing the wrong that was being done.

to this country. Because a storm had occurred in the Northwest only once in twenty years, the people to whom the paper was sent, which did not mention that fact, would suppose that it was the usual occurrence, just as the writer of that article A-efiecting on the district of Alberta as a ranching country did not say it occurred only once in twenty years, but would have the impression go forth that it was the usual occurrence in Alberta, and that the district around Saskatoon was preferable for raising cattle. Speaking of Southern Alberta, the paper said :
. It is said by those familiar with both places that Saskatchewan is a better and more certain ground for ranching than southern Alberta. In the latter place blizzards come suddenly, and as no shelter is provided, often ninety per cent of a drove is lost in a single snow storm.
The hon. gentleman who represents the district of Alberta sat silent when the statement was made about his country ; and yet he pretends to be an honest representative of the people of that district. In the Agriculture Committee, because he forms an unfavourable opinion of Mr. Macoun, he wants to fight everybody in sight. The hon. gentleman had better confine himself to his own district, and not wander so far afield.
You had better do that yourself.
The district from which I come does not need any defence. But I have some interests in that very country about which I am speaking.
Not very much.

I think they are pretty extensive ; from my standpoint they are at least ; and I am interested in not havifig that country defamed. That is my excuse for speaking on this occasion, if any excuse is needed. The wrong in this attack is that this paper goes out with a stamp of government approval. I was a little surprised tonight at hearing the hon. Minister of the Interior, in speaking of this matter, try to shift the responsibility on his officers ; but he did not say that he would see that the officer who was responsible for allowing that paper to go forth in that shape would be castigated or even reprimanded, as Mr. Preston was for having written that letter. Notwithstanding that, he said it was perfectly right that these statements should go forth. You want to induce farmers from tile United States to settle in the Northwest Territories, and you do it by saying that in Southern Alberta, one of the most important districts of the Northwest, ninety per cent of the cattle are destroyed by reason of the blizzards that often rage throughout that district. It seems to me the hon. member for Alberta has to-night given a most pitable exhibition in sitting silent and not until the lash was applied to him would he
rise and say a word on behalf of the district which had been so abused and maligned by the documents which had been distributed by the government of which he is a supporter, a thick-and-thin supporter- an hon. gentleman who professed at one time to be an independent member, and who has developed into one of the most ardent thick-and-thin supporters of the government that can be found within their ranks. He wanted to inflict violence on those who; disagreed with him in the Agricultural Committee in regard to what was said by Mr. .Macoun with respect to the little-known and sparsely settled Peace River district, and yet to-night he sits mild as a cooing dove and listens to this abuse of his own district of Alberta.

The hon. member made some reflection on my candour. He said he would rather be accused of lack of mentality than lack of candour. I think he has given evidence to-night that he is as lacking in candour as in mentality, and that he is absolutely lacking in both. I am sorry that my conduct in this House has not the approval of the hon. gentleman ; but as I did uot come here under his approval, I will try to suffer under his disapproval. I am here at the approval of the district of Alberta, the district which he says has been maligned by the reading of a quotation from the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' by the hon. member for Saskatchewan. If there could be anything more absurd than that statement, it would be the whole attitude and action of the hon. member himself and the part he has taken in this debate to-night. The hon. gentleman is surprised that I sat silent. Well, certainly this House would be surprised if he sat silent and also more greatly surprised if he talked sense when he did not sit silent.

I do not think the hon. gentleman has succeeded in saying anything very clever, although of course he drew, forth a cackle from the back benches over there. So far as mentality and candour are concerned, I would be prepared to be judged by a competent jury, but I would hardly consider these gentlemen on the back benches as competent to give a verdict. In neither respect would I care to be reduced to the low level of the hon. gentleman, and I am confident that a comparison of the speeches made by both of us, as shown in the * Hansard,' would prove that the hon. gentleman has occupied at least ten times longer the time of this House during this, or any other session when we both occupied seats in this House, than I have.
I would go still further and would guarantee that in the one-tenth of the time I have talked, as compared with the .time the hon. gentleman has taken up, I have talked a thousand times more sense than he did in ten times longer time. No one has yet been able to discover in any speech the horn

gentleman lias made one single, solitary, minute portion of sense. He is looked upon by the great majority of this House, not excluding a great many of the members on the other side, as a sort of mountebank.

I only wish to refer, not to what the hon. gentleman has just said, but to the allusion he made to my action in the Agricultural Committee. He said I was anxious to use physical force in that committee. I want to say here and now that in that committee, in defence of the district I represent and the people I represent against attacks made by an officer of this government and other members of that committee who sit before me, I was compelled to risk the application of physical force to myself by those hon. gentlemen and take chances upon it or else to submit to just such bullying and just such abusive language as the hon. gentleman has undertaken to deal out to me tonight.
