I have in my hand an article which perhaps the hon. member for Alberta may have read. The Toronto ' News ' had the hardihood to express an opinion about that hon. gentleman, and I find in the Edmonton ' Bulletin ' language of this kind. I do not say that the hon. member penned the article, but after I read it, perhaps hon. members will come to a conclusion as to who is responsible. Speaking of the 'News' the ' Bulletin ' says :
Its reputation based on its short and not over brilliant career under its present management Is that of a cross between an attempted bandit and a would-be thug. That is one who-speaking in a literary sense would rob for profit and murder from principle-always providing the opportunity were favourable.
I do not say that the ' Bulletin ' is the hon. gentleman's paper. If it is not, he is in a position to deny that it is.
Does the hon. gentleman deny the description given there of the Toronto 'News'?

All I have to say Is this, that the editor of that paper is in my judgment as competent to edit a paper as the hon. gentleman is. I can tell him more, that the leader of the great party he is supporting will corroborate my statement.
I notice that the hon. gentleman's answer is entirely non-committal.

I thought I was answering fully and fairly. I think that the management of the Toronto 'News ' is quite capable of answering any editorials that appear in this paper. In respect to the immigration litei'ature-or campaign literature, for it seems to me to be about the same thing nowadays-I find that the Department of Immigration has paid the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' $7,000 for a paper issued by that concern. Now, if the Department of the Interior were doing its duty.
It would not allow any literature intended to be used for immigration purposes to be sent out without scanning every line to see whether the circulation of it is in the interest of this country. So, I say that when the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) allows the government to circulate at the public expense a newspaper which states as a mere rumour something derogatory to his constituency, he is not doing his duty to those who sent him here, nor is he displaying the energy which he displays when Mi\ Macouh. a government officer made a report about his part of the country. Is that lack of energy due to the fact that there are a couple more senatorships being' given to the Northwest, or is it because there is an edition of 5,000 immigration pamphlets being published by the Edmonton ' Bulletin ? ' This pamphlet, the newspapers tell us, comprises 80 pages profusely illustrated with scenes from the. district and business places of Edmonton and with portraits of many of the leading men of the town. I wonder if the hon. gentleman himself would be included. These pamphlets, I understand, are to be distributed in the United States and Great Britain. So we have $7,000 for this edition of the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' and we have an edition of 5.000 copies coming from the Edmonton ' Bulletin ' Office. Is there anything for the Regina ' Leader ? ' Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) say that there is any of this patronage for the ' Leader ? ' Now, is this system in the interest of the people ? Is it in accordance with sound policy to dole out payments for immigration literature as patronage to favoured people in the Northwest Territories ? The government has its printing bureau here. If they would furnish that printing bureau with better facilities why could not all that work be done there ?
Then, what would become of the papers ?

I do not know, but I do know what would become of some of the
independent men of this House. Instead of their submitting to the discipline mentioned by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) we should find them with the old frankness and outspokenness of the hon. member for Alberta, not moved by considerations of immigration pamphlets or senator-ships.

I do not know whether hon. gentlemen opposite think they can (lo in this House as they thought to do in the Agricultural Committee, prevent me from expressing myself and defending my position bv bullying and interruptions They were not successful there, nor will they be here Nor will they succeed by piling up misstatements in regard to myself or throwing out vile insinuations, a thing ot which we find them to be very capable. Though they may judge other people by their own standards we have to consider where these things come from. In regard to the state meats made deliberately by the hon. member for East Elgin that in the Agricultuial Committee I threatened Mr. James M. Ma-coun with horse-whipping I wish to say that that statement is absolutely untrue.
I say it is true.
I said that Mr. James M. Maeoun deserved horse-whipping, and I say so still. But I did not say that either I or anybody else was going to horse-whip him.
You knew better than to try it.

That is a sample of the argument placed before the Agricultural Committee, during sitting after sitting, in support of Mr. James M. Maeoun in discrediting a large and important section of the Northwest Territories. I am glad these hon gentlemen have brought the discussion into this House, so that the country may be well informed of the position.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would draw the attention of the hon. member (Mr. Oliver) to the fact that I have ruled that the discussion that took place in the committee cannot be referred to here. We have to deal with the items before us. What took place in the committee is past and gone and we have nothing to do with it.

I will observe your ruling, Mr. Chairman. Now, I may refer to the insinuations of the hon. gentleman as to the pamphlets printed in the ' Bulletin Office. I am connected with the Edmonton * Bulletin.' This is a matter not worthy the consideration of this committee, but seeing that an hon. member has brought it forward, I suppose it is only fair that the facts should be known. The connection of the Edmonton ' Bulletin ' with the pamphlet is this : Mr. Sutter, who is the Immigration agent at Edmonton has seen fit to get up an immigration pamphlet as a speculation

of his own. That pamphlet, I understand, is being paid for by the merchants of Edmonton who are taking advertising space in it. The 'Bulletin' was successful in getting the contract for the printing of the pamphlet from Mr. Sutter. The 'Bulletin' does not know the government in the transaction in any way, shape or manner, and I am not aware that Mr. Sutter knows the government in the transaction in any [DOT]way, shape or manner.
Is he a government employee ?
He is, but I am not aware that he is getting government assistance in getting out this pamphlet.
Are you aware that he is not ?

No, it is none of my business. But I know that he has solicited a considerable amount of support from Edmonton business men to get out the pamphlet, which is designed, I believe, for free distribution. It is a custom in the progressive towns in the Northwest to get out pamphlets in just such a way as this and place them where they will do the most good, distributing them amongst the government immigration agencies as far as *possible. That is what, I understand, lias taken place in regard to that pamphlet. So far as its being a matter of government patronage, I am not aware that the government have anything to do with it. I am only aware of it to this extent, that I understand the ' Bulletin ' had to compete for the work of printing the pamphlet.

I would like some statement from the minister on that point. It seems there is being a pamphleL got out for distribution for immigration purposes by a government employee at Edmonton, Mr. Sutter, and that it is being printed by the Edmonton ' Bulletin.' I would like to know if the government are purchasing that pamphlet or paying any consideration for it ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know anything about it. I never heard of it before. *

The opposition seem to be in a jubilant mood to-night; there efforts have been great in the last two days. They have talked a great range of subjects ; they have discussed dog-tisli. a live earl, fat chickens and sore eyes, and now they want to talk blizzards. Now with reference to this discussion about the district of Alberta, my hon. friend from King's, N.B. (Sir. Fowler) tried to make out that I had said something disparaging to the district of Alberta. I want to say that I did nothing of the kind.
I merely read a portion of an article that was written by some resident of the district of Saskatchewan living close to Saskatoon. The hon. member for Marquette took exception to this supplement in the Manitoba J Free Press ' that has been circulated, say-

ing it cast reflections upon the country. This is an article written about the Calgary and Southern Alberta district. It was doubtless written by some resident of Alberta Here is what this article says :
Calgary, September 20th. One week of steady, fine weather, such as sunny Alberta is famous for, has settled the crop question which has been the leading topic of conversation in this territory for many a week.
Here is where the member for Marquette gets his work in. He underlines the following :
The lateness of the season was alarming, but after the fall storms

He stopped at the ' fall storms.'
-there has come the usual fall sunshine, during which the grain has ripened bountifully, and the farmer has harvested with ease. The climate of Alberta is once more vindicated and the crops are fully up to expectation. The districts around Calgary, from Innisfail to the northern frontier, have harvested their 400 bushels of wheat, 1,500 bushels of oats and 200 bushels of barley, all of an excellent quality, to the quarter section.
Why did he not read that part of it ? He underlines again the following :
The slight frost of the last storm

And stops there, he did not read the next line.
-is found to have done very little damage.
He took good care to mention the frost, but he did not take such good care to say that there was no damage done by that frost.
The production of wheat is light because in the country around Calgary the cultivation of it has been almost given up, although the yield per acre averaged much over 20 bushels.
I submit that is a very good article about the district of Southern Alberta. I do not see anything wrong in that.
Does he mean to say that an article stating that they have almost given up the cultivation of wheat is a good article to distribute amongst intending immigrants ?

I have not heard of any immigration agent advising any person to go to Calgary 'to raise wheat, they advise people to go there to raise cattle. It is a good ranching country as well as a good wheat country. The writer of this article goes on to say :
The farmers simply found that other grain was more profitable.
They went out of wheat raising, because they could make more money growing barley and oats.
As to oats, there will be many phenomonal crops. Some farmers claim as much as 75 bushels to the acre.

Does the hon. gentleman want anything better than that ?
-but the average appears to be really about 40 bushels to the acre. The barley is pronounced all right by those farmers who arg least disposed to boast of their wealth. There has been an immense Increase in the acreage over past years, but for obvious reasons of the large immigration as well as of the progress accomplished by those previously settled, it will be much larger next year.
The whole of that article is a good article. This writer mentions frost, of course. He says there was a slight frost, but it did no damage. The hon. member for Marquette read there was a frost, but he left out the part that said there was no damage.

I placed on the ' Hansard ' more than what is underlined there, as the hon. gentleman will find on reading ' Hansard ' to-morrow. I read out a great deal more than he has read himself now. There is a great deal underlined that I did not read.

If he was quoting from this paper, I hope he did not read anything that wasn't in it. I think that Is a very good article about Alberta. I don't think any one could write a better article. But the hon member for Marquette garbles the article, he reads a portion and leaves out a portion. He does not read the portion where the writer says it did no damage. He has picked out a few lines to serve his purpose. A man may make a paper say almost anything by picking out a few words here and there. The Bible says there is no God, if you only read a portion of it.
The Bible does not say that. It is the fool who says that.

I say that you can read out of the Bible that there is no God. But, take the line before that aud the Bible says :
' The fool hath said in his heart there is no God.' My hon. friend from Marquette takes this paper, leaves out a few lines here and a few words there, and garbles its contents for the sake of earning for himself, I suppose, a little kudos in his own constituency, but he must be hard up for an argument against the hon. Minister of the Interior or the immigration branch when he can find nothing better than that. If there were 200,000 copies of that paper circulated and if they cost this country $7,000 I think, judging from the number qf desirable people who have been brought into this country the money was well spent and I do not think that it is open to any person to say anything against it. The hon. member for King's New Brunswick (Mr. Fowler) tried to place In my mouth words that I did not say by attributing to me the statement that I said something derogatory of southern Alberta when he knows that I did not say anything of the kind. I merely read an extract from
a letter written by a gentleman who is enthusiastic about the southern district of Saskatchewan and who says that southern Saskatchewan is a better district in which to raise cattle than any other part of the Northwest Territories.

I said that the hon. member for Saskatchewan read this from the paper for the purpose of contrasting the two districts and he has done the same thing now. That is what I said as ' Hansard ' will show.

I wish to draw the attention of the committee to the statement made by the hon. member for Saskatchewan and to compare it with that made by the hon. member for Alberta. The hon. member for Saskatchewan has stated that he approved of the publication of these 200,000 copies and of scattering them broadcast throughout the American union to be paid for by Canadian money. As to the storm what did he prove by that ? I would draw his attentiou to the fact that the ' storm ' does not refer to the storm of the 12th September alone but refers to storms occurring in May as well and that this paper refers to storms, frosts, &c., more than forty times in the same issue. While the hon. gentleman says that is perfectly true, what does the hon. member for Alberta say ? He says that he would not take up the time of the House in denying such an idiotic rumour, that it was absurd, that he dismissed it as unworthy of credence, a statement written by some anonymous person from the Saskatchewan district which he did not think it worth while to make a denial of in this House. Yet the hon. member for Saskatchewan says it is absolutely true. When he quoted this letter from Saskatchewan he also backed it up by stating distinctly that it was true that in some of these storms seventy-five per cent- I remember particularly that he got fifteen per cent below what the correspondent had put it at-of the cattle perished.
Is that true or not ?

It is absolutely untrue and I am condemning the government for distributing this literature and paying $7,000 for. the purpose of libelling the country. While the hon. member for Alberta states that I am more responsible for having had it placed in ' Hansard,' even if it were true and denounces me for it it was this hon. gentleman who wrangled by the hour and contended that it was quite in order to have what he called libellous statements published-and distributed broadcast in reference to his own Peace river country. How very consistent that hon. gentleman is ! The hon. gentleman will acquiesce in using public money for the purpose of paying $7,000 to the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' when there was no necessity for that edition, scattering it broadcast and telling the people

735$
of the United States that there was a most exceptional storm on the 12th September,
that the crops were damaged and that the farmers conld only cut their grain if at all in one way. He is prepared to justify that. If we are spending our money for immigration literature we do not desire to say what is untrue or to publish a libel on the country. Although that hon. gentleman would not defend his constituency to-night, although he would not say that this statement is untrue 1 say that it is untrue as far as my knowledge goes. Although not a resident of the district I have a sufficient knowledge of it to know that there have been no storms In it in which ninety per cent of the cattle were destroyed. Again I say I denounce this statement as untrue and I say that it is to be regretted that so many thousands of dollars of our money were paid out for the purpose of sending broadcast through the American union a libel upon our country which could only injuriously affect the immigration which we expect to get. In proof of that I have only to say that the hon. gentleman who placed those papers before me stated that he had a letter from a family in the United States who wrote that they had intended to emigrate to Canada until they read the .description of this storm in that literature.

The anxiety which hon. gentlemen opposite show for the welfare of Southern Alberta is very touching. I am sure it will appeal to the people of that favoured district very much. It would be a very sorry thing for southern Alberta as well as the Northwest Territories if they had to depend upon hon. gentlemen opposite for good will or good report. In regard to the' results, of the publication of this $7,500, copy of the ' Free Press ' and the fear that is expressed by the hon. member for Marquette it may relieve his mind on that point if I tell him that the immigration to Southern Alberta this year, according to the best information given to me, is larger than to any other part of the Northwest Territories not excepting Northern Alberta, so that if there is any application of this edition of the ' Free Press ' to the district of Southern Alberta that suggestion and that allegation made by the hon. member for Marquette and other hon. gentlemen have been absolutely disposed of by that fact.
They could not have read it.

Showing that the argument they have adopted was as unfounded as their intention was unfair. I here make the statement once more that this hon. gentleman has on his responsibility as a member of parliament representing a western constituency placed upon the pages of ' Hansard ' statements which are deliberately garbled and wffien read in * Hansard ' will lead any person to believe, if they believe Mr. W. J. ROCHE.
the hon, gentleman at all, that the country is not the country that it is or ought to be in order to attract settlers. The hon. gentleman has taken that position in this House, he has taken it deliberately and with malice aforethought simply and solely for the purpose of attacking a member of the government who has done so much to make the Northwest

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman, as I understand it, makes a statement that my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) deliberately and with malice aforethought did so and so.

Exactly.
Mr. SrROULE. Is such a statement in accordance with parliamentary rules of debate ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) did state that another hon. gentleman had made a statement deliberately and for the purpose of misleading it is certainly unparliamentary.
Mr. OLIVER, Even if it is true ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.
Well, I will withdraw it even if it is true.
As a usual thing I pay little or no attention to the Billingsgate that the hon. member for Alberta usually furnishes this House with. I do not propose to descend to that.
Order.
I do not think I am out of order at all.
Is the hon. gentleman in order in using the word Billingsgate ?
I am quite in order and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) should be the last man in the House to take exception to my remarks.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rule is that an hon. member cannot say to another hon. member, anything other than one gentleman would be supposed to say to another.
I presume the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) is not subject to that rule.

If there is any man in this House who indulges in offensive language to members on this side, it is the hon. member for Alberta. When any one differs from his views, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) cannot combat it in ordinary ianguage, but he must descend to such language as the hon. member (Mr. Ingram) read from the Edmonton ' Bulletin ' in reference to the Toronto ' News.' The hon. member (Mr. Oliver) has changed, his

opinion in regard to the ' Free Press.' He defends it to-night, but a short time ago referring to the ' Free Press ' in the Edmonton ' Bulletin, ' he referred to it as a journalistic prostitute. In view of the language he can indulge in, I do not think there is any lecture coming to me from the hon. member for Alberta.

This all proves that the Department of the Interior should carefully scan every line of literature that is circulated for the purpose of promoting immigration. The hon. gentleman from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) accused the member for Marquette of deliberately garbling this literature, notwithstanding that my hon. friend (Mr. Roche) denied it.
I don't think he denied it.
I will deny it now, if you are not satisfied.

If we who indulge in honest criticism can take exception to language in this literature, how very likely it is that those opposed to immigration to Canada will use it for their own purpose. I understood from the Minister of the Interior that he rather approved of this literature.
The hon. member for Marquette stated that he did not want to publish an untruth, but at the same time he did not want to publish the truth.
I absolutely deny that I said anything "of the kind.
I have no hesitation in saying that under certain circumstances it would not pay us to spend public money-to publish the truth about such things as this.

I was eight years in the parliament of Nova Scotia before confederation ; I have been a representative in this House for a number of years, and I must say that the style of debate I have heard to-night is no credit to either one side nor the other. Surely we ought to remember that we are gentlemen in this House, and that these contradictions from one side to the other should be avoided. This style of debate is sickening.

The Minister of the Interior says he has never heard of this publication by the Edmonton ' Bulletin. ' What we want to know is whether it is the intention of the department to pay for the whole or any portion of this literature.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I answered I had never heard of it before.
That is not an answer to the question.	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman wait till I get through ? I said I never heard of it before and that we had no intention of paying for it.
I am glad to hear that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I made it before.
Is it the policy of the department to allow one of its agents to issue literature for circulation abroad,_ promoting immigration to any particular section ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I see no objection to that. Of course if it were brought to our attention we would not permit a statement derogatory to any other district.

That is after the literature is published. You would lock the stable door after the steed is stolen. Unlike the Liberal opposition before 1896, there is not a gentleman on this side of the House who objects to voting money for a wise expenditure on immigration. When we placed items for immigration in the estimates before the Liberal opposition told us that the expenditure was too large.
Because you got no results from it.
You paid for literature before it was printed and it was never circulated, although the man got the money.
Please give an instance.

Prior to 1896, when the exmember for Assiniboia was proprietor of the Regina ' Leader,' you paid him $2,000 and you were to receive several thousand copies of his paper to be circulated abroad. You paid him the $2,000 before it was printed. You never got a paper to circulate abroad, and he charged at the rate of $22 per column for inserting in connection with the fair held at Regina, the breeding of the different horses that were entered in the speeding ring at the horse races. I remember that one item calculated to attract immigration to the Northwest Territories was the entry of a race horse named Skyscraper, bred out of Thunderbolt and sired by Spinaway. This thing was investigated by the Public Accounts Committee, and there are members opposite to-night who opposed the commissioner's report censuring that sort of thing.
Is that the whole truth ?
Absolutely, because I examined the witnesses myself before the committee and the evidence is on record.
Is the hon. gentleman as truthful about this as he was about the duty on corn.
I was truthful about the duty on corn and I am truthful about this. The hon. gentleman was mistaken about the duty on corn, but I thought I had given him enough information to make him wise.
The answer of the government he supports contradicted his statement, and bore out my statement on that matter!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope hon. gentlemen will not get on the corn question now.

The hon. gentleman has made a statement in regard to the Regina ' Leader ' and the contract with the late member for West Assiniboia. I understand that that gentleman sold out to my hon. friend who is now the honoured representative of that constituency.
He did not sell out until long after.

My hon. friend from Regina, I understand, bought that paper from the late representative of West Assiniboia, with that contract included ; and when the hon. gentleman took over the plant, he did not include the contract.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken. That was concerning the printing of law reports.
Perhaps it may be as stated by the hon. member for South Essex. My toon, friend from West Assiniboia is here, and he will bear out whether it is correct or not.

If I may be permitted to say so, I do not very much relish this item which has been brought into the discussion. As far as that is concerned, except as to the amount, the statement of the hon. member for South Essex is absolutely accurate. I think it was $400 or $500 in place of $2,000.

I am afraid my hon. friend is cornered again. What I want to find out from the Minister of the Interior is the policy of the government in issuing immigration literature. The hon. gentleman to-night noticed a discussion in which certain members of this House are charged with garbling immigration literature. I want to ask him if he allows his agents to issue immigration literature in any town in the Dominion of Canada without first submitting it to the hon. gentleman or his officers ? If anything is wrong in that literature, how can he conscientiously right the wrong that may be done by having the literature circulated. The hon. gentleman says he has no objection to any immigration agent providing any literature.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have no rule in regard to the matter to which my hon. friend has referred. I believe there have been three or four oases in which agents of the department have assisted in preparing literature for the district in which they were doing the work. Mr. Sutter, the agent at Edmonton, is a very capable and satisfactory agent, and if he asked to be allowed to prepare a pamphlet, I would not have the slightest objection to his doing so. If afterwards he said something in the pam-Mr. INGRAM.
phlet which was improper or incorrect, he would be censured for it in the same way as any other officer.

I think that is a very dangerous policy to adopt. If the immigration department had strong opposition from the railway companies of the United States, some of the employees might be tempted to issue immigration literature t[iat would be very injurious to Canada. Every line of immigration literature prepared by any officer of the government should be submitted to the department and the department should be held responsible for the issue of proper literature. The policy at present pursued is a dangerous policy.

I quite endorse the statement made by the hon. member for East Elgin. I think a great deal of care should be exercised in the selection of the literature that is published and sent abroad either to the United States or Great Britain, so that only proper literature shall be sent out. I deprecate the idea of allowing private individuals to prepare matter of this kind. But we some times find objectionable literature issued even under the superintendent. I hold in my hand a volume which has been sent out from the Interior Department with the compliments of the superintendent of immigration at Ottawa, and on one page of this volume I find this :
Corby's IXL Rye Whisky, Purity Rye Whisky, Canadian Rye Whisky, Three Government Standards ; Corby's Famous Whiskies, distilled and bottled in bond by H. Corby, distiller, Belleville.
Is it necessary to have this kind of matter put into immigration literature ? I do not think it is worth while to use the money of the country to pay for literature of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What is the name of the book to which my hon. friend is referring ?

The ' Canadian Year Book ' for 1904, distributed by the Immigration Department. I merely point this out to show that the Immigration Department is not exercising, a proper superintendence over the literature it is sending out. This book contains a great deal of useful information, but this is not the kind of literature which should be sent abroad through the government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is a sort of a year book issued by a private individual. I -do not remember seeing a copy of it before. I remember at the time it was issued we paid something for an advertisement in it.. I think that that is the extent of the connection the Department of the Interior had with it. The circulation, I think, was guaranteed to be so many, and we paid something for the advertising. I am quite unable to see anything improper in that. It

is not departmental duties. The hon. gentlemen are suffering apparently for want of ammunition if this is all they can discuss.

I suppose we will have to submit to the hon. gentleman's statement, but I want to draw his attention to this. The paper was issued May 24, 1904, and the bottom part of the paragraph says it is designed for the use of immigration agents in the United States and in the old country, an edition of 5,000 being printed for this purpose. It is only fair to the committee that a gentleman who is in the employ of the government should submit these documents for the consideration of the committee. I do not think it is right that an agent in any part of Canada should have the right to get up an advertising medium under the guise of an immigration pamphlet and send it out to all parts of Canada, the United States and Great Britain, without the department or somebody authorized by the department examining into it and finding out whether it is in the interests of the people this document should be sent out for immigration purposes. Will he say to whom in Ottawa this agent sent some copies, because no doubt it is in circulation at present ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know. I have not seen the document, I do not know what is in it. I am not responsible for what appears in the Edmonton ' Bulletin.' As my attention has been called to the statement that the pamphlet has been written by Mr. Sutter, I will give instructions to have him written to. But I am satisfied to have him write a description of Alberta and the department may be just as responsible as if it had been prepared here in Ottawa in the department itself. I have every confidence in Mr. Sutter's ability.

Motion agred to, and House adjourned at 1.30 a.m.-Friday.

Fkiday, July 22, 1904.
